docs.title: JATMP documentation
docs.text:
JATMP is a self-hosted platform for spotting cyber threats and online fraud as they emerge. It reads security news, social media, threat-intelligence platforms and scam and fraud sources, and keeps track of:

  • Cyber threats: malware and ransomware families and their campaigns, threat actors, vulnerabilities (with CISA KEV, EPSS and CVSS context), ATT&CK techniques, and indicators of compromise checked against intel providers. → Analysis
  • Scams and fraud: scam types such as investment and loan fraud, phishing, malicious APKs and crypto drainers, as well as impersonated banks, e-wallets and government bodies, scammer identifiers and reported losses. → Scams and fraud
  • Critical infrastructure: the sectors each item concerns, following Indonesia's Perpres 82/2022. → Analysis
  • Geography: target, source and hosting countries, Indonesian provinces, and an International / National (Indonesia) view across the whole interface. → Geography and Indonesia

Everything goes through one pipeline into one connected set of entities, so a scam report links to the malware it installs, and a ransomware campaign to the CVEs it exploits. Two dashboards show the results, one for cyber threats and one for scams and fraud, and the data can be shared through the REST API, STIX / TAXII, IOC feeds, webhooks and MISP.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text: This page gives an overview of how JATMP turns collected items into entities, scores, verdicts, correlations and trends. The exact rules, weights and formulas are in How it works, especially Severity scoring, Enrichment and verdicts and Trends and correlation.

docs.title: Entity extraction
docs.text:
Every item is searched for malware families (about 150, plus their aliases), threat actors (about 45), CVEs, ATT&CK techniques and indicators (IPs, domains, URLs, and MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 hashes).

Defanged indicators are understood in all their usual forms (hxxp, [.], [:], [://], \., (dot)). Families that aren't in the knowledge base yet are picked up from phrases such as "PipeMagic backdoor", but legitimate tools that attackers misuse (ConnectWise, AnyDesk, PsExec and others) are never mistaken for families. Family names that are also everyday words ("Play", "Hook") need a qualifier such as "ransomware", unless they are written in the family's own spelling ("RedLine", "Cl0p").

JATMP also ignores hashes that are part of a URL, version numbers that look like IP addresses, public DNS resolvers such as 8.8.8.8 and 1.1.1.1, and about 200 vendor, media and platform domains. Paste, file-sharing and code-hosting services (Pastebin, GitHub, Google Drive, Dropbox, MEGA and others) are handled carefully: the service's own domain is never an indicator, but the URL of a specific paste or file on it is.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Every item gets a score from 0 to 100 that explains itself: the item page shows the full breakdown.

The signals are grouped (exploitation, impact, threat class, activity) so that synonyms aren't counted twice. Within a group, the strongest term counts in full and the runner-up at half weight, and terms in the title count 1.5 times as much as terms in the body. Patch notes, round-ups, guides and routine leak-site victim postings are scored down. When an indicator is later confirmed malicious, the items that mention it are scored up.

When a new version changes the scoring rules, every stored item is re-scored once after the upgrade, so old and new items are always judged the same way. Re-scoring keeps the points that enrichment and the AI added.

docs.title: Cross-source enrichment
docs.text:
Indicators found in news and social posts are looked up on whichever of these providers you have keys for: VirusTotal, OTX, urlscan, ANY.RUN, MalwareBazaar (hashes), URLhaus (URLs, hosts, payloads), GreyNoise and AbuseIPDB (IPs). Each provider works at its own pace, so a slow one doesn't hold up the others.

The answers are combined into a single verdict:

  • Any provider reporting malicious wins.
  • Infrastructure that OTX whitelists is marked clean.
  • A lone mention in an OTX pulse is treated as suspicious rather than malicious.
  • GreyNoise acts as a false-positive filter. An IP it knows as a benign business service or benign scanner is marked clean, unless a strong provider (VirusTotal, abuse.ch, ANY.RUN) says otherwise. Mass scanners get a "mass scanner" badge, because their activity is opportunistic rather than targeted.

Failed lookups are retried after six hours, and unknown results are checked again after three days. When a provider identifies a family (for example, a hash on Bluesky identified as Lumma Stealer), the indicator is linked to that family, so it connects to every article about it. For trending families, JATMP also pulls fresh indicators from OTX and ANY.RUN, using only pulses that actually name the family.

Verdicts age. IPs, domains and URLs change owners, so every verdict carries the date it was last confirmed. A malicious or suspicious one that is still being mentioned is checked again after 30 days, and the new answer can lower it. If it isn't confirmed within 60 days, the indicator drops out of the IOC export feeds. File hashes never age.

The IOC page and Settings → Enrichment show how many indicators are waiting to be looked up and how much of each provider's daily budget is left.

An analyst can also set an indicator's verdict by hand. That verdict wins over the providers until it is undone (see below).

docs.title: Corrections and rule quality
docs.text:
No set of rules is perfect, so analysts and admins can correct JATMP's mistakes, and the corrections stick:

  • ✕ next to an entity on an item page removes it from that item ("Pegasus" in an article about a musical).
  • ✎ Correct on an entity page removes a family or actor everywhere, marks an indicator as not a threat, or sets an analyst verdict (malicious, suspicious or clean).
  • Not a scam report, in the fraud-score popover of an item, takes the item out of the scam section.

Each correction asks for a reason and records who made it. Re-extraction, the AI and rule changes don't bring the mistake back, and the affected items are re-scored. The Corrections page lists every correction with an undo button, the error rate analysts reported per area over the last 30 days, and the names corrected most often, which usually point at a rule worth tuning.

The rules themselves are measured too. python manage.py quality reports the precision and recall of the extractor, the scam rules, sectors, target countries and severity on a set of labelled cases, and CI fails when a change makes any area worse. Analysts' corrections can be exported as test cases, so the report also says how many of the mistakes analysts found the current rules would still make. Details are in Corrections and quality.

docs.title: Relationship graph
docs.text:
Item and entity pages show an interactive graph: the item, its entities, whatever enrichment linked them to (a hash to its family, an indicator pulled from OTX), and other items that share them. Nodes are coloured by type and verdict. Click a node to preview it, double-click to open it, drag and zoom to explore, or use the keyboard (Tab, Enter, O). The graph is drawn by a small built-in SVG renderer rather than a third-party library. It starts with up to 60 nodes, and Show more raises that to 150.

A second row in the legend explains each kind of line in the graph and whose claim it is: Mentions (automatic), Provider link (a provider's claim), and Also mentions and Mentioned together, which are marked needs validation because they only come from appearing in the same items. Hover a legend entry or a line for the explanation; see Reading the lines.

docs.title: Infrastructure context, on demand
docs.text:
Context lookup on an IP, domain or hash asks Shodan (open ports, host names, known CVEs), Censys (services, network owner), CrowdSec CTI (reputation, behaviour), Pulsedive (risk, threats), Hybrid Analysis (sandbox verdict and family) and IPinfo (network owner and country, used for the geography features), as far as you have keys for them.

Their free tiers are small, so these lookups never run in the background unless you switch on run context lookups when an indicator turns malicious. Shodan InternetDB and IPinfo can be used without a key once keyless lookups are allowed.

docs.title: Correlation
docs.text: The item page ranks related items by how strong the evidence they share is. A shared hash, URL or domain counts for far more than a shared CVE, rare entities count for more than frequently mentioned ones, and items from another source or source type get a bonus. Newsletters and round-ups, which name many unrelated things in one issue, count for much less and are marked digest. Entity pages show coverage per source, the entities mentioned alongside it (leaving newsletters out), related indicators, and enrichment results. On an indicator's page the provider links (Linked by enrichment) come first, and the co-mentions are called Seen in the same items as, because appearing in the same report is not attribution. See Correlation.

docs.title: Trends
docs.text:
The dashboard scores each family, CVE and threat actor by how often it was mentioned in the chosen period compared with a baseline before it (30 days, or as long as the period when that is longer), weighted by how many sources and source types cover it. A story that several outlets carry counts once.

The results appear on the threat radar (one icon per type), in a chart over time, and in the Trending malware, Trending CVEs and Trending threat actors tables, which also list the families, actors and CVEs mentioned alongside each entry.

Two breakdowns put the period in context:

  • CVEs by exploitation risk places each CVE in the first bucket it qualifies for: in CISA KEV, EPSS of 10% or more, CVSS critical (9+), high (7 to 8.9), or lower. CVEs with no CVSS score and a low EPSS, or not looked up yet, are counted below the chart.
  • Threat actors by type counts stories per kind of actor: nation-state, ransomware, extortion (data theft and extortion crews such as ShinyHunters or Scattered Spider) and cybercrime. Actors from the built-in knowledge base are already classified; others are unclassified unless data/knowledge_extra.json gives them a category.

docs.title: Critical infrastructure sectors
docs.text:
Each item is tagged with the critical information infrastructure sectors it concerns, as defined by Indonesia's Perpres 82/2022 (Infrastruktur Informasi Vital): government administration, energy & mineral resources, transportation, finance, health, ICT, food, and defence.

The rules (app/processing/sectors.py, in English and Bahasa Indonesia) look for the organisations and services of each sector as targets or affected parties: rumah sakit and hospitals, banks and e-wallets, airlines and bandara, telecom operators and data centres, ministries, pemda and .go.id sites, refineries and PLN, the military and TNI.

A sector counts when the title names it or the body names it at least twice. Newsletters and round-ups only count their title, and look-alikes are excluded (MITRE's defense evasion, the hacktivist IT Army). A sector stated by the feed (the ransomware.live victim sector, OTX industries) counts on its own. An item gets at most three sectors.

Sectors are entities like any other (of type sector). They appear as chips, filter the feed (click a bar in a Critical infrastructure sectors chart) and the scam report list, and are exported as sectors in the REST API. They carry almost no weight in correlation. When the rules change, stored items are re-tagged once; python manage.py sectortag does it by hand.

docs.title: Vulnerability context
docs.text:
Every six hours, the CVEs mentioned in the last 30 days are looked up in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue, FIRST EPSS and the NVD (CVSS score, vector and description). None of these needs a key; an optional NVD key just makes the CVSS lookups faster.

Trending CVEs are ranked by exploitation risk as well as by how much they are discussed: trend score × 2 if in KEV × (1 + EPSS) × (0.5 + CVSS/10). The CVE list can be sorted by CVSS or EPSS.

CVSS rates how much damage a flaw allows if it is exploited (0 to 10). EPSS is the probability that it will be exploited in the wild within the next 30 days. Hovering over either column header shows the same explanation.

docs.title: A note on severity
docs.text: The severity score is a triage aid, not a vulnerability rating. The item page shows how each score was built. Enrichment raises it when an indicator is confirmed malicious (and lowers it again if that verdict is later withdrawn), the AI can raise it by a limited amount during analysis, and an analyst's correction re-scores the item from the entities that remain.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: This page explains how JATMP is put together: the process model, what happens on start-up and on every request, how an item travels from a feed into the database, how background jobs work, and where each concern lives in the code. The tables and columns are described in Data model; step-by-step recipes for common changes are in Extending JATMP. The behaviour of each process — the exact rules, weights, thresholds and timings — is described in How it works.

docs.title: The big picture
docs.text:
JATMP is a single Python process: a FastAPI web application with an APScheduler BackgroundScheduler running in the same process. There is no message queue, no separate worker and no front-end build step.

browser, API client
        │ HTTP
        ▼
┌─ one process: run.py → uvicorn ──────────────────────────┐
│                                                           │
│  FastAPI: middleware → routers → Jinja2 pages / JSON      │
│        │                                                  │
│        ▼                                                  │
│  SQLAlchemy ◀──▶ SQLite (WAL) or PostgreSQL               │
│        ▲                                                  │
│        │                                                  │
│  APScheduler threads                                      │
│    ├─ collectors → pipeline.ingest                        │
│    │     → extractor, severity, fraud, sectors, geo       │
│    ├─ enrichment → intel providers → consensus            │
│    └─ CVE intel, summary, housekeeping, webhooks,         │
│       one-off re-analysis                                 │
│        │                                                  │
│        ▼                                                  │
│  app/netguard.py: every outbound request                  │
│  (SSRF guard, size cap)                                   │
└────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         ▼
     internet: feeds, providers, AI, MISP

Consequences of this design that every change has to respect:

  • One web worker. The scheduler lives in the process, so running two workers would run every collector twice. Scale collection by source intervals, not by workers.
  • Threads, not processes. Collectors and enrichment run in the scheduler's thread pool (10 threads). A job that blocks (a slow provider, a regex that backtracks) holds one of those threads; it cannot be killed. Keep network timeouts short, keep regular expressions linear (see Security), and push slow side work (AI summaries) into a job of its own.
  • One writer on SQLite. WAL mode lets the web pages read while a job writes, but writes are serialised. Long jobs commit in chunks (usually 200–500 rows) so that pages and other jobs are not blocked for long.
  • In-process caches are per process. The settings cache (5 s), the trending cache (45 s), API-key rate windows and manual-action throttles live in memory and reset on restart.

docs.title: Start-up sequence
docs.text:
app/main.py defines the FastAPI app and a lifespan handler. On start:

  1. init_db() (app/db.py) creates missing tables, adds missing columns and indexes (_add_missing_columns, see Database and migrations) and sets up full-text search (app/search.py).
  2. If the install is not finished (data/config.json has installed: false), the setup token is announced in the log (app/setup_token.py) and nothing else starts. Every request except /setup, /static and /healthz is redirected to the wizard.
  3. Otherwise:
    • new built-in sources are added (setup_service.auto_seed_sources);
    • secret settings written in plain text by older versions are encrypted (settings.encrypt_stored_secrets);
    • private hosts the admin already configured are put on the outbound allow-list once (netguard.seed_allowlist);
    • jobs.start() schedules one job per enabled source, the periodic jobs and the one-off re-analysis jobs, then starts the scheduler.

The same perform_install() (app/setup_service.py) is used by the wizard, by install.py and by the test suite's installed fixture.

docs.title: Request lifecycle
docs.text:
1. SessionMiddleware (outermost) decodes the signed jatmp_session cookie into request.session. Sessions are stateless: the cookie holds uid, sv (session version), csrf and a few UI choices (dashboard period, region).
  2. setup_guard middleware redirects to /setup before installation, creates the per-request CSP nonce (request.state.csp_nonce) and adds the security headers to the response (CSP, X-Frame-Options, nosniff, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, COOP, Cache-Control: no-store, HSTS when JATMP_SECURE_COOKIES=1).
  3. Router dependencies (app/auth.py):
    • current_user returns the built-in local user in single-user mode; in multi-user mode it loads the user from the session and rejects disabled users and sessions whose sv no longer matches users.session_version (raises LoginRequired, which an exception handler turns into a redirect to /login?next=…).
    • require("viewer" | "analyst" | "admin") checks the role on top of that.
    • verify_csrf checks the synchroniser token on every non-GET request: the X-CSRF-Token header (sent by app.js for data-post buttons) or the csrf_token form field.
    • The REST API uses api_v1.principal(scope) instead: a Bearer (or Basic) API key with the right scope, or the browser session.
  4. The handler works with a SQLAlchemy session from get_db() (closed after the request) and returns either web.render(request, "page.html", ctx) or a dict (JSON).
  5. web.render adds what every template needs: app_name, multi_user, csrf, nonce, path, region. Templates extend base.html; inline <script> blocks must carry nonce="{{ nonce }}" or the CSP blocks them.

Everything that leaves JATMP (REST API, IOC feeds, STIX / TAXII, webhooks, MISP pushes) goes through the rules in app/sharing.py (TLP, redistribution) and never includes scammer identifiers (fraud.IDENT_TYPES).

docs.title: From a feed to the database
1. Collection
docs.text:
jobs.run_source(source_id) is scheduled every interval_minutes per enabled source (and queued by Run now / Collect now). It looks up the collector class by Source.kind in collectors.REGISTRY, calls fetch() -> list[RawItem], and records the run as a CollectorRun row (running → ok, skipped or error). A collector raises SkipCollector when it cannot run for a known reason (no API key); that is not an error and does not notify.

RawItem (app/processing/pipeline.py) is the only thing collectors produce:

Field Meaning external_id Stable id of the entry within its source (GUID, post URI, pulse id). The dedup key. title, url, author, content, published_at As the provider gives them. content of kind="article" is HTML and gets stripped; posts are already text. kind article, post, pulse, scan or analysis. Affects stripping, dedup across sources (articles only) and severity. tags Provider tags (OTX tags, hashtags). On intel sources they may name malware families. raw Small provider metadata kept on the item (tlp, sector, industries, listed_by…). Bulky copies of the content are dropped. indicators IOCs the feed delivers as structured data (pulse indicators, blocklist entries), already typed.

docs.title: 2. Ingest
docs.text:
pipeline.ingest_committed() wraps ingest() in a transaction and retries on IntegrityError (the scheduled collector and a backfill may store the same entry at the same moment). For every new RawItem, ingest():

  1. Skips duplicates of the same source: one query for the whole batch on (source_id, external_id). External ids longer than 500 characters are shortened with a SHA-256 so they stay unique. An entry that is already stored but carries a merge_title (ThreatFox's one item per family and day) has its new indicators added to the stored item instead (merge_indicators), which is then re-scored.
  2. Sanitises: strip_html (scripts, tags, entities, stray stylesheet rules) for articles, safe_url (only http(s) links), length limits, future dates clamped to now.
  3. Fingerprints articles (fingerprint(): normalised title without the outlet suffix, plus the start of the text for short titles) and marks a syndicated copy of another source's article from the last four days with dup_of.
  4. Extracts entities (extractor.extract_all): IOCs (refanged, strict mode for news: only defanged indicators or link targets count), CVEs, ATT&CK techniques, known families and actors from the knowledge base, new family names by pattern ("Zorblax ransomware", Indonesian "ransomware Zorblax"); plus the feed's structured indicators and family names from intel-feed tags (tag_families).
  5. Scores severity (severity.score_item): explainable 0–100 with reasons, see Analysis.
  6. Fraud analysis (fraud.apply): scam types, impersonated brands, scammer identifiers, losses, victims and the fraud score, see Scams and fraud.
  7. Sectors (sectors.apply): critical infrastructure sectors.
  8. Links entities (link_entities): one lookup query per entity type, new entities created in one flush, ItemEntity rows with the origin of each extraction, mention_count and first_seen / last_seen maintained.
  9. Blocklist verdicts (mark_listed) for curated lists such as ScamSniffer.
  10. Geography (geo.tag_item): language, source country, target countries and Indonesian provinces.

After the commit the trending cache is cleared, and jobs._after_ingest queues webhook events and the MISP auto-push; _maybe_auto_summarize queues AI summaries for the separate summary job.

docs.title: 3. Enrichment
docs.text: jobs.run_enrichment (every enrichment_interval minutes) picks indicators that were never checked, are due for a re-check, or have an aged malicious / suspicious verdict (verdict_recheck_days). enrichment.prefetch then looks the whole batch up with one thread per provider, so each provider works at its own pace, and enrichment.enrich_entity applies the answers one indicator at a time: every configured provider in PROVIDER_CLASSES that supports the indicator type answers with a LookupResult; results are stored per provider in enrichments, family labels are mapped to known families (resolve_family) and linked (entity_links), and the provider verdicts are combined into the entity's verdict (_consensus: malicious wins, a lone OTX mention is only suspicious, GreyNoise "benign" overrides noisy providers) with its date in verdict_at. A verdict that rises adds severity.VERDICT_BONUS to the items that mention the indicator and, when it turns malicious, fires the ioc.malicious webhook; a re-checked verdict that falls takes the bonus back (_sync_bonus). Trending families also get fresh IOCs from OTX / ANY.RUN (enrich_family). enrichment.queue_status and intel/quota.py feed the queue and quota panels. Details: Enrichment and verdicts.

docs.title: Background jobs
docs.text:
All jobs are functions in app/jobs.py.

Job Trigger What it does run_source every interval_minutes per source; manual Collect and ingest one source run_enrichment every enrichment_interval min; manual Look up indicators with the providers run_cve_intel every 6 h; manual CISA KEV, FIRST EPSS, NVD CVSS into Entity.meta run_webhooks every 30 s Deliver queued webhook events with back-off run_digest daily, digest_time (default 06:00 UTC) AI executive summary run_housekeeping daily, housekeeping_time (default 03:30 UTC) Retention (slimming, deletion), identifier pruning, old runs and notifications run_auto_summaries after ingest, when enabled AI summaries of new high-severity items, one job at a time run_backfill manual Historical backfill, one source after another run_source_health hourly (first 15 min after start) Notify about quiet and long-failing sources (app/sourcehealth.py) run_geoip_update monthly, when enabled Refresh the offline GeoIP database One-off re-analysis 15–90 s after start See below

The daily jobs run in the schedule's time zone (schedule_timezone, jobs.schedule_daily_jobs); they are rescheduled when the General settings change. At start-up, requeue_auto_summaries rebuilds the in-memory auto-summary queue from the live items of the last 24 hours that still qualify.

Runs and progress. Every run is a CollectorRun row. Manual runs are created as queued rows under a batch_id first, so the UI shows them at once and a second click finds them (job_running, active_batch). Progress is kept in memory (_live, written by _progress) and served by jobs.status() to /api/jobs/status, which app.js polls. When the last run of a batch finishes, _maybe_finish_batch writes one notification for the whole batch. Runs left queued or running by a restart are marked aborted on the next start.

Versioned one-off jobs. When detection rules change, stored items have to be re-analysed once. Each such job compares a rules version constant with a value in the settings table and does nothing when it is up to date; it runs a few seconds after start and can be forced from the UI or manage.py.

Job Version constant Setting What it redoes run_content_cleanup jobs.CONTENT_VERSION content_version Text cleaning of stored items run_geotag geo.GEO_VERSION geo_version Language, targets, provinces, IP hosting country run_dedup jobs.DEDUP_VERSION dedup_version Cross-source fingerprints run_fraudtag fraud.RULES_VERSION fraud_version Scam types, brands, identifiers, fraud score run_sectortag sectors.RULES_VERSION sector_version Critical infrastructure sectors run_digesttag digest.RULES_VERSION digest_version Newsletters and round-ups (Item.is_digest) run_rescore_if_outdated severity.RULES_VERSION severity_version Severity from text and linked entities, keeping the enrichment bonus and AI assessment (severity.carry_over); runs last, at 90 s

Entity extraction has no automatic job: changing it only affects new items until an admin runs python manage.py reextract (which rebuilds the extracted links and re-scores, also through carry_over).

docs.title: Outbound HTTP
docs.text:
Every request JATMP makes on its own goes through netguard.client() (app/netguard.py), directly or through Collector.client(), intel.clients._client(), intel.cve._client(), intel.darkweb._client(), the MISP client, the LLM client, the GeoIP download and webhook delivery. The client:

  • only reaches public addresses; private, loopback and link-local hosts need an entry in the outbound_private_hosts setting (webhooks use their own webhooks_allow_private switch);
  • checks every redirect hop, and connects to the address it checked (a custom httpcore network backend), so DNS rebinding does not work;
  • reads bodies through a response hook that stops after max_bytes of decompressed data (20 MB by default);
  • behind an environment proxy (HTTPS_PROXY…) checks the request URL instead, because the proxy resolves the name.

Never call httpx.get() or create an httpx.Client directly in application code.

docs.title: Database and migrations
docs.text:
• Engines. SQLite (default, data/jatmp.db, WAL, foreign_keys=ON) or PostgreSQL via JATMP_DATABASE_URL (postgresql+psycopg://…). python manage.py copy-db URL copies one into the other.
  • Sessions. SessionLocal has expire_on_commit=False and autoflush=False. Routes get a session from get_db(); jobs open SessionLocal() themselves and close it in finally; scripts and tests use session_scope() (commit on success, rollback on error).
  • String lengths. A before_flush hook trims strings to the column length, because PostgreSQL rejects what SQLite accepts.
  • Migrations are forward-only and automatic. create_all creates new tables; _add_missing_columns adds columns that a model declares but the table lacks (with the column's scalar default, so existing rows get a value) and creates every declared index with checkfirst. There is no Alembic. Consequences: never rename or drop a column in a release, give new columns a default, and write a versioned one-off job when existing rows need computed values.
  • Full-text search. SQLite: an FTS5 table items_fts kept in sync by triggers. PostgreSQL: a GIN index on to_tsvector('simple', title || ' ' || content). Both are created by search.ensure_fts(); queries go through search.item_text_clause(), which never passes user input into the query syntax.

docs.title: Front end
docs.text:
Server-rendered Jinja2 templates in app/templates/, one stylesheet (static/css/app.css, theme tokens for dark and light) and plain JavaScript files with no build step. Because of the CSP there are no inline event handlers; behaviour is attached through attributes handled in static/js/app.js:

Attribute Behaviour data-post="/api/…" POST with the CSRF header, show the message as a toast, optionally data-target (inject HTML), data-reload, data-busy data-confirm="…" Ask before a form or button submits data-preview="/items/1/preview" Open a partial page in the side drawer (_preview_item.html, _preview_entity.html) data-tip="…" Explanation tooltip

Charts use the vendored Chart.js; the radar and sparklines are in motion.js, the relationship graph in graph.js, the maps in geomap.js and the dashboard globe in globe.js (pre-projected outlines in static/geo/, rebuilt by scripts/build_geo.py).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: API keys and options are managed under Settings, which requires the admin role. You can also put them in a .env file next to run.py (see .env.example), which is loaded automatically. A value set through an environment variable takes precedence over the interface, and Settings shows it as locked.

docs.title: API keys
docs.text:
Every provider is optional. JATMP uses whichever ones you configure and skips the rest.

Service Variable Notes VirusTotal VT_API_KEY The free tier allows 4 requests a minute and 500 a day. JATMP keeps to both (vt_min_interval, vt_daily_budget) AlienVault OTX OTX_API_KEY Free. Subscribe to pulses or users on OTX, so that the "subscribed" feed has content urlscan.io URLSCAN_API_KEY The Search API needs a key. On a free account, search task.tags:malicious (the default) rather than verdicts.malicious:true, which needs a paid plan ANY.RUN ANYRUN_API_KEY Needs a plan that includes TI Lookup; the base URL can be changed in Settings. The TI Lookup endpoint (/v1/intelligence/api/search) hasn't been tested against a real key yet, so the parser is written defensively abuse.ch ThreatFox ABUSECH_AUTH_KEY Free (an Auth-Key from auth.abuse.ch) abuse.ch MalwareBazaar, URLhaus ABUSECH_AUTH_KEY The same free Auth-Key as ThreatFox NVD NVD_API_KEY Optional. CISA KEV, FIRST EPSS and the NVD all work without a key; with one, CVSS lookups are faster (50 per run instead of 10). CVE lookups can be switched off entirely under Settings → Enrichment GreyNoise Community GREYNOISE_API_KEY Free, with a small daily quota (greynoise_daily_budget, default 40) AbuseIPDB ABUSEIPDB_API_KEY The free tier allows 1,000 checks a day (abuseipdb_daily_budget, default 900) ransomware.live RANSOMWARELIVE_API_KEY A free PRO key, required for use by organisations. Without it, JATMP uses the personal-use API (one request per minute per endpoint) Hudson Rock Cavalier HUDSONROCK_API_KEY A free key, used for the infostealer deep dive Shodan SHODAN_API_KEY Optional. Without a key, the free InternetDB is used (once you allow keyless context lookups) Censys CENSYS_API_TOKEN, CENSYS_ORG_ID A Platform personal access token; free accounts get a small monthly credit CrowdSec CTI CROWDSEC_API_KEY Free tier Pulsedive PULSEDIVE_API_KEY Free tier Hybrid Analysis HYBRID_ANALYSIS_API_KEY A free (vetted) account IPinfo IPINFO_TOKEN A free Lite token. Without one, the keyless endpoint is used (once you allow keyless lookups) Offline GeoIP MAXMIND_LICENSE_KEY Optional. Download GeoIP database (Settings → General) or manage.py geoip-update fetches the DB-IP IP to Country Lite database (no account needed, CC BY 4.0) into data/geoip/. With a MaxMind key it fetches GeoLite2 Country instead. A monthly refresh can be switched on in Settings MISP MISP_URL, MISP_API_KEY The automation key of a MISP user. Distribution, sharing group, TLS verification and auto-push are under Settings → MISP X / Twitter X_BEARER_TOKEN API v2 is a paid service. Alternatively, set rss_bridge on each X source Telegram (optional) TELEGRAM_API_ID, TELEGRAM_API_HASH, TELEGRAM_SESSION Not needed for public channels with a web preview. For MTProto you need an application from my.telegram.org, requirements-telegram.txt, and a one-off python manage.py telegram-login (see Sources) AI model LLM_PROVIDER, LLM_BASE_URL, LLM_MODEL, LLM_API_KEY Optional.
