docs.title: AI processing
docs.text:
This page explains what the optional AI features do, what they send to the model, and the safeguards that stop a model's output from overriding the rule-based analysis. Setting up a model is covered in Reporting and AI. The code is in app/llm/insights.py, app/llm/client.py and app/llm/redact.py.

When the AI is set to Off (the default), none of this runs and nothing is sent anywhere. The rest of JATMP works exactly the same without it.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
1. The rules decide; the model adds. Severity, entities, verdicts and fraud scores come from the rule-based pipeline. A model can write a summary, suggest extra families, actors and tags, and raise a severity by a limited amount. It can't push a score below what the rules gave it, remove an entity or change a verdict.
  2. Article text is untrusted. Whatever a model reads was written by someone else, and it may contain instructions aimed at the model ("ignore the above, severity 100"). So everything the model extracts from the text is checked against the text and the rest of the data before JATMP uses it.
  3. AI output is labelled. Entities and tags suggested by the model carry an AI badge, and its severity points appear as a separate reason (AI assessment (capped)).
  4. Prompts stick to the data. Every prompt tells the model to use only the material it is given, to say when information is missing, and never to invent indicators or scammer identifiers.
  5. Personal data stays out of cloud prompts. Phone numbers, bank accounts and similar details are replaced with placeholders before a prompt goes to a cloud model (see What leaves your network).

docs.title: Item summaries
docs.text:
A summary is written when someone clicks Summarise on an item (limited per user and per minute), or by the auto-summary queue.

What the model receives: the item's kind, the source's name and type, the title, publication date and author, the entities already extracted (up to 40), and the text (up to 12,000 characters).

What it is asked for, in two parts:

  1. One line of JSON listing the malware families named in the text (with a category), the threat actors, a severity from 0 to 100, and tags such as phishing or supply-chain.
  2. After a --- line, a brief of no more than 350 words in the configured language: a TL;DR, key points, who or what is targeted, delivery and TTPs (with ATT&CK ids only where they are clear), and ideas for detection and mitigation.

The brief is saved as the item's summary. When let the LLM discover malware families is on (the default), the JSON part is applied as well, after these checks:

Suggestion Accepted when Stored as Malware family (up to 10) The name appears word for word in the item's text and is no longer than 60 characters, and either it is a known family (mapped to its official name), or it passes the extractor's plausibility checks (not a generic word, tool, platform, country or everyday word) and the item comes from an intel source or another source already mentions that name A link with origin llm Threat actor (up to 10) It appears word for word in the text, and it is either a known actor, or plausible and already mentioned by another source A link with origin llm Severity The model's number is higher than the rule-based score Raised by the difference, at most +20. The model's number is stored with the reason, so a later re-score can apply the same assessment again Tags (up to 10) After unusual characters are removed, each is at most 40 characters Added to the item's tags; new ones are also noted as AI tags

When an item is analysed again, the previous AI assessment is taken off first and the new one replaces it. A lower new assessment can therefore remove points, but the score never drops below what the rules gave it.

The result is that a new family name from a single news article is ignored until a second source reports it, and a name the model made up is ignored because it isn't in the text.

docs.title: Auto-summaries
docs.text:
When auto-summarize new high-severity items is on (it is off by default) and a model is configured:

  1. After each collection run, the new items join an in-memory queue of at most 200 ids (when it is full, the oldest drop off). Backfilled items are not queued.
  2. A single job, run_auto_summaries, starts 2 seconds later. Further collection runs only add to the queue; they never start a second job.
  3. The job summarises up to 10 items per run, skipping items with severity below 40, items that already have a summary, and syndicated copies.
  4. As soon as one summary fails (the model is down, slow or out of quota), the job stops, so it doesn't run the whole queue against a broken model. The next collection run starts it again.
  5. Because the queue lives in memory, it is rebuilt at start-up from the items that would still be in it: live items collected in the last 24 hours with a severity of 40 or more, no summary yet, and not a copy, most severe first (up to 200).

Summaries never run inside a collection run. A slow model (JATMP waits up to 300 seconds for an answer) would otherwise tie up a collector thread for a long time.

docs.title: Threat briefs
docs.text:
Generate brief on an entity's page (for analysts and admins) writes a brief of about 450 words, based on:

  • the 25 most recent items that mention the entity in the last 60 days (source, date, title, and the summary or the first 600 characters of the text);
  • every provider's enrichment answer;
  • the 15 families, actors, CVEs and techniques most often mentioned with it;
  • up to 30 linked indicators, with their verdicts.

The brief has these sections: overview, recent activity and campaigns (with dates and sources), infection chain and TTPs, targeting, notable indicators (only from the data provided), ideas for detection and hunting, and an assessment of whether activity is rising and how confident that assessment is. The brief is saved on the entity and shown until someone generates a new one.

docs.title: Executive summary
docs.text:
run_digest runs daily at 06:00 by default, when the daily summary is switched on, and also whenever someone clicks AI summary. You can change the time and the time zone under Settings → General (digest_time and schedule_timezone). The default is UTC, which is 13:00 in Jakarta, so a team there would typically choose Asia/Jakarta and a time such as 07:00. The next scheduled run is shown on the same tab.

The input is calculated by JATMP's normal statistics, not by the model:

Data Details Trending malware The top 8 of the last 7 days, with recent and baseline counts, sources, growth and the new flag Trending actors The top 5 Trending CVEs The top 6 by priority, with KEV, CVSS and EPSS Scam types The top 5, with reports this week and the week before, and whether they are spreading Sectors Up to 5 sectors with items this week Top items The 25 original (non-copy) items of the last 24 hours with the highest severity plus half their fraud score, each with its summary or the first 220 characters of its text

The output the model is asked for is a single JSON object: a one-sentence headline, an overall threat level (low, elevated, high or critical), 3 or 4 key points (each a title and one sentence), and no more than 3 actions for today.

Before it is shown, JATMP checks the answer. It extracts the JSON, removes Markdown formatting, bullets and maths notation from every text, limits the lengths (headline 400 characters, point titles 120, details 400, actions 300), keeps at most 4 points and 3 actions, and drops a threat level it doesn't recognise. If there is no usable headline, the model's text is shown as it came. The result is saved under AI insights, shown on the dashboard card, and announced with a notification. If the run fails, an error notification is sent (at most once a day).

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Ask (on the AI insights page) answers a question using the collected data:

  1. Which items. llm/retrieval.py scores the items of the period the question names ("today", "minggu ini", "this month"; otherwise the last 30 days), copies of a syndicated story left out:

    Signal How it is found Weight Entities the question names Families, actors, CVEs and indicators by the extractor (aliases included: "Fancy Bear" is APT28), scam types and brands by the fraud rules 4 Concepts A malware type ("ransomware", "stealer", "pencuri data"), a critical infrastructure sector ("hospital", "rumah sakit", "bank"), or a question about scams 2 Words Each word of 3 or more letters (common English and Indonesian words left out, up to 8) through the full-text index; an item doesn't need every word 1, plus 0.5 when it is in the title

    "Ransomware attacks on hospitals" therefore finds "LockBit hits a healthcare provider" although they share no word. When nothing matches, the most severe recent items are used so the model can say what there is. 2. The 25 best items, numbered [1]…[25], each with its summary or first 500 characters, and the top 10 trending families are added to the prompt. 3. The model is told to answer only from that material, to cite the items it uses as [n], and to say what is missing. 4. Each citation becomes a link to the item, and under the answer Based on N item(s) lists the items with what the question matched (entities, concepts, period); items the model did not cite are greyed.

It is still not a search by meaning (embeddings would be the next step), but synonyms that JATMP already knows (aliases, sectors, malware types) now carry the question. Answers are saved under AI insights and deleted after 90 days.

docs.title: What leaves your network
docs.text:
With a local model (Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, vLLM and similar), prompts stay on your own infrastructure. With a cloud provider, the prompts described above are sent to that provider: item titles and text, entity names, enrichment summaries and statistics. These requests go through the same outbound guard as everything else (see Security).

Personal data is replaced before a prompt leaves. Item text can quote the phone numbers, bank accounts and e-mail addresses of scammers and victims. Before a prompt goes to a cloud model, JATMP replaces:

  • every phone and e-wallet number;
  • every account number written as such ("rekening BCA …");
  • every run of 10 to 18 digits (national ID numbers, card numbers, account numbers);
  • every e-mail address.

Each one becomes a placeholder that stays the same for the same value within a prompt, such as [phone 1], [account 1], [number 1] or [email 1], so the model can still tell them apart. Amounts written with separators ("Rp 1.500.000"), IPs, domains, hashes, CVE ids and crypto wallets are left alone, because they are what the analysis is about. Summaries of redacted items therefore mention the placeholders, not the numbers.

The setting Personal data in prompts (llm_redact, Settings → AI) controls this:

Value Behaviour cloud (default) Redacts when the model runs outside your network: Anthropic, or an OpenAI-compatible or Ollama server on a public host name. Localhost, private addresses, and single-label or .local / .internal names count as local always Always redacts, even for a local model never Never redacts

docs.title: Collection
docs.text: This page explains how sources are scheduled, what each collector fetches on a run, how runs are tracked and reported, how JATMP notices a source that has stopped working, and how a manual collection or a historical backfill differs from the normal schedule. For the list of built-in sources, see Sources.

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text:
Every enabled source gets its own scheduled job (source:<id>), which runs jobs.run_source. These rules apply:

Rule Value Why Interval The source's interval_minutes, at least 5 The built-in defaults are 30 minutes for Bluesky and Mastodon, 60 for most RSS feeds, and 180 for fraud feeds, X and ThreatFox First run after start-up 5 s + 3 s × source id Spreads the first wave out, so dozens of sources don't start in the same second Overlap A source never runs twice at the same time A slow feed can't pile up runs Missed runs Merged into one, as long as it is no more than 10 minutes late After a pause the source catches up once, not once for every missed turn Threads All jobs share one pool of 10 threads A provider that hangs blocks one thread, not the whole platform

When you edit, enable or disable a source under Settings, its job is rescheduled (or removed) straight away. Deleting a source removes its job and its items.

Collectors never decide when they run; they only know how to fetch. Every request they make goes through JATMP's outbound guard (app/netguard.py), which only allows public addresses unless you allow-list a host, checks every redirect, stops reading a response after 20 MB (after decompression), and gives up after 30 seconds. See Security.

docs.title: One run, step by step
docs.text:
run_source(source_id)
 │
 ├─ 1. create or claim the run record ............ status "running"
 ├─ 2. collector.fetch() .......................... phase "fetching"
 ├─ 3. pipeline.ingest_committed(raw items) ....... phase "storing"  (see Ingest and analysis)
 ├─ 4. update the source's status
 ├─ 5. side effects of the new items .............. webhook events, MISP auto-push
 ├─ 6. close the run .............................. status "ok", "fetched N, new M"
 └─ 7. queue AI auto-summaries .................... only when enabled
  1. Run record. A run record (CollectorRun) is created and set to running. For a manual batch, the record that was already queued for this source is used instead.
  2. Fetch. The collector for the source's type asks the provider for its current list of entries. See What one run fetches.
  3. Ingest. All entries go through the pipeline in a single transaction, and only new ones are stored. Progress ("storing 40/100") is updated every five entries.
  4. Source status. The source's last status, last error and last run time are updated. You can see them on the Sources tab.
  5. Side effects. For the newly stored items, JATMP queues webhook events (item.high_severity, entity.watched) and, if misp_autopush_min_severity is above 0, starts a MISP auto-push. If anything goes wrong here it is logged, but the run itself still succeeds.
  6. Close. The run is closed with its status, a short message and the number of new items.
  7. AI. If auto-summaries are on and an AI model is configured, the new items join the summary queue, which has its own job (see AI processing).

Some collectors remember a little between runs so they only ask for what is new: Mastodon keeps the account id, X keeps the user id and the last post id it saw, and the OTX, MISP and ransomware.live collectors ask for what changed since their last run.

docs.title: Run outcomes
docs.text:
Status What it means Source status Notification ok The run fetched and stored entries. Zero new items still counts as ok ok None for scheduled runs skipped The collector can't run for a known reason: a missing API key, no handle or URL, Telegram not signed in skipped None. A manual batch says how many were skipped error Anything else: an HTTP error, a feed that can't be parsed, a timeout, a rate limit (429) error, with the message Once, when a scheduled run goes from working to failing (Source failing: …). After 24 hours of failures, a daily reminder follows until it recovers (see Source health) aborted The process stopped while the run was queued or running, or someone stopped a backfill unchanged None queued / running Still in progress. Status views treat a record that has been in these states for over 3 hours as dead — —

If a run fails while fetching or storing, everything it stored is rolled back. A source therefore adds either a complete batch or nothing at all, and the next scheduled run simply tries again.

docs.title: Source health
docs.text:
A source can stop working without ever reporting an error. A feed that has moved may return an empty page, or a site that blocks JATMP may return a normal-looking response with nothing in it. Every run is then ok with zero new items, and nobody notices.

To catch this, JATMP looks at each source's live items and its last 30 days of run history (app/sourcehealth.py), and shows the result next to the source on the Sources tab:

Figure How it is worked out Last new item When the source last brought in a live item (backfills don't count) This week · usual Live items from the last 7 days, compared with the weekly average of the 4 weeks before. It is marked below usual when it drops under 30% of that average (for sources that usually bring at least 5 a week) Usual gap The median time between runs that brought something new. It needs at least 3 such gaps before it shows a value Failing for How long ago the current run of failures started Summary only The source's news items average fewer than 400 characters of text. The feed only carries summaries, so extraction and severity scoring have little to work with

Every hour, jobs.run_source_health checks two conditions and sends a notification (at most once per source, condition and day):

  • A source is quiet when it has brought no new item for 3 times its usual gap, and at least 12 hours.
  • A source has been failing for 24 hours or more.

The Sources tab also lists the sources that need attention above the table.

docs.title: What one run fetches
docs.text:
Each scheduled run asks the provider for its current list. Entries that are already stored are skipped during ingest, so overlap between runs only costs a little bandwidth.

Type One scheduled run fetches Item kind Notes rss The feed (up to 10 MB). The first 500 entries are read, the topic filter is applied, and the newest 100 are kept article (post for social sources) The text is the entry's full content if the feed has it, otherwise its summary. The article page itself is never opened bluesky The account's last 50 posts, without replies post Public API, no key needed mastodon The account's last 40 posts, without replies post The account id is remembered after the first run x The last 50 posts through API v2 (only ones newer than the last post seen), or the configured RSS bridge post Skipped without a bearer token or bridge. A 429 rate limit counts as an error telegram The latest page of the channel's public web preview (20 posts), or the last 50 messages over MTProto post Posts without text are skipped otx Subscribed pulses changed since the last run (3 days on the first run), up to 50; or one pulse search (30 results) pulse Up to 300 indicators per pulse come in as structured indicators. The pulse's TLP, targeted countries and industries are kept urlscan One search, 100 results. The default query is task.tags:malicious AND date:>now-1d: scans tagged malicious in the last day scan The URL, domain and IP of each scan come in as indicators. The old default, verdicts.malicious:true, can't be searched on free accounts and failed with 403 Forbidden; sources created with it keep their saved query until you edit it anyrun One TI Lookup query over the configured period (7 days by default), 100 tasks analysis Never shared outside JATMP (provider terms) threatfox IOCs from the last day, grouped into one item per family per day (up to 300 IOCs per run) pulse The day is the day ThreatFox first saw the IOCs. If a later run finds new IOCs for a family and day that are already stored, it adds them to that item, updates the count in its title and scores it again. No new item is created, so no new webhook event is sent ransomwarelive The 100 most recent victims, or the full list for one country or group (keeping posts newer than the last run minus 2 days) post The victim's website is deliberately left out of the text: it belongs to the victim and is not an indicator misp Events changed since the last run minus 1 hour (the last days days on the first run, 7 by default), 50 per page, up to 5 pages pulse The event's TLP is kept; attributes become indicators scamsniffer The daily list files of the last 4 days (the public list is published a week late) article One item per day. Its domains are marked malicious as soon as they arrive

Intel sources (category intel) are handled a little differently during ingest: indicators are taken from plain text, not just defanged text, and their tags may name malware families. See Ingest and analysis.

docs.title: Topic filters
docs.text:
Any news or social source can have a topic filter (filter in its configuration): RSS feeds, Telegram channels, X, Mastodon and Bluesky accounts (since 0.13; it used to exist for RSS only, so a general Telegram channel brought in everything). Intel feeds don't offer it. The filter runs on what a collector fetched before anything is stored (processing/topics.py, for scheduled runs and backfills alike), so entries it drops leave no trace; the run message says how many were off topic ("fetched 40, 31 off topic, new 9").

Filter Keeps an entry when Used for security A security term (English or Indonesian) appears in the title, the first 3,000 characters of the text, or the tags General technology sections cyber An unambiguous cyber or digital-fraud term appears, or the scam analysis recognises a scam General news sections and general Telegram or X channels, where words like "bocor" or "modus" usually mean something else fraud The scam analysis recognises a scam Fact-checkers, whose feeds are mostly about political hoaxes

The source topic scam & fraud is a separate setting. It doesn't filter anything. Instead it tells the scam analysis to treat the source's items as likely scam reports (a single scam word is enough for Other scam), and it lists the source on the fraud overview.

docs.title: Runs, batches and progress
docs.text:
• Scheduled runs create their record when they start and close it when they finish.
  • Manual collection (Collect now, Run now, manage.py collect) first creates one queued record per source, all sharing one batch id, and then starts the runs. The status bar shows the whole batch, for example "Collecting… 12/40 sources · 85 new". Clicking again while it runs finds the active batch rather than starting a new one, and Run now on a source that is already running is ignored.
  • Progress (fetching, storing N of M, the phase of an enrichment run) is kept in memory and served to the page, which polls it. It isn't written to the database during the run, so it never competes with the run's own writes.
  • Batch summary. When the last run of a batch finishes, one notification sums it up, for example "Collected 85 new items from 40 sources, 2 errors", with the names of the sources that failed and how many were skipped. Inside a batch, the per-source Source failing notification isn't sent.
  • Restarts. At start-up, every run that was still queued or running is marked aborted ("interrupted by a restart"). Nothing resumes half-way.

docs.title: Backfill
docs.text:
A backfill (Manage → Backfill) fetches history instead of the current list. It works like this:

  1. One queued run is created for each selected source, all in one backfill batch.
  2. A single worker goes through them one at a time. Backfills are long, and SQLite only allows one writer at a time, so sources are never backfilled in parallel.
  3. For each source, the collector says what it can do: whether it supports backfill, how, and how far back. Sources that can't be backfilled are skipped, and the start date is limited to how far the source can reach (7 days for ThreatFox, for example).
  4. The collector returns entries page by page. Each page is stored and committed on its own, marked as backfill, so a backfill that is stopped or fails keeps everything it already stored.
  5. Stop cancels the queued sources straight away and lets the current source finish the page it is on.
  6. One notification sums up the batch.
Collector How far back it can go RSS on a WordPress site The site's REST API returns every post in the range (100 per page), so the estimate is exact Other RSS Internet Archive snapshots of the feed (one a day), filtered to the range. You only get what the feed listed when it was archived Bluesky / Mastodon The account's history, paged back with the API's cursor (up to 6,000 posts / 4,000 statuses per account per run) Telegram Older pages of the web preview (up to 3,000 posts), or MTProto (up to 5,000) OTX / MISP Subscribed pulses or events changed within the range ThreatFox The API's limit of 7 days ransomware.live (country or group source) The full victim list, back to 2021 for most groups ScamSniffer One archive file per day, back to 31 May 2022 X, urlscan, ANY.RUN, ransomware.live recent Not supported (quota-limited or recent-only)

Backfilled items keep their original publication dates and are marked as backfill. Their indicators are only sent to the enrichment providers if the item is from the last 14 days or enrich_backfill is on (see Enrichment). They don't trigger webhooks, MISP pushes or AI summaries, and they don't count towards source health. They do count in statistics and trends, by their original dates, so last year's history fills the longer dashboard periods without making anything trend today. See History and storage.

docs.title: Corrections and quality
docs.text: Every rule-based system makes mistakes. This page covers how analysts correct JATMP's mistakes, how those corrections stay in force, and how the detection rules are measured so a rule change can be judged by its effect. Code: app/corrections.py and app/quality.py.

docs.title: Analyst corrections
docs.text:
Analysts and admins can correct four things. Each correction asks for a reason, is recorded with the analyst's name, and can be undone.

Correction Where What it does Wrong entity here ✕ next to an entity on an item page Removes that one link (a family, actor, CVE, sector, scam type, brand or indicator) and re-scores the item Wrong entity everywhere / Not a threat ✎ Correct on an entity page Removes the entity from every item, re-scores them, and stops it being linked again. An indicator also becomes clean Analyst verdict ✎ Correct on an indicator page Sets malicious, suspicious or clean. It wins over the providers: later lookups still store their answers, but they don't change the verdict. The items that mention the indicator get or lose the enrichment bonus with it Not a scam report The fraud-score popover on an item page Sets the fraud score to 0 and removes the item's scam types, brands and identifiers

docs.title: Why a correction sticks
docs.text:
A correction is not a one-off edit, because the jobs that rebuild things would bring the mistake back. Instead the active corrections are consulted wherever that could happen:

Job that could undo it What stops it Re-extraction (manage.py reextract), AI extraction, the ThreatFox merge, new items link_entities skips links an analyst removed: one item's link for wrong entity here, every link for wrong entity everywhere Scam re-analysis after an upgrade, Re-analyse items The fraud analysis gives an item marked not a scam report a score of 0 Enrichment and the re-check of stale verdicts An analyst verdict is kept; its date is refreshed by each lookup, so it does not age out of the feeds while the indicator is still mentioned Re-score all items, the severity rules version Severity is computed from the links that remain

The active corrections are cached in memory for at most 30 seconds and reloaded at once after a change.

docs.title: The Corrections page
docs.text:
Corrections (in the sidebar) lists every correction with who made it, when, why and its target, and has an Undo button for each active one. Undoing restores what the correction changed: the removed links come back with their original origin, an indicator gets its previous verdict back, a scam report is analysed again.

The page also shows two things for the last 30 days:

  • Error rate reported by analysts: per area, the links analysts removed against all links made in the period, and the items marked not a scam report against all scam reports. It is a lower bound, since it counts only the mistakes someone noticed.
  • Most corrected: the names corrected most often. A name that keeps coming back usually needs a rule change, for example an everyday word added to COMMON_WORDS in the knowledge base (see Extending JATMP).

Every correction is also written to the audit log (correction_unlink, correction_verdict…, and correction_undone).

docs.title: Measuring the rules
docs.text:
python manage.py quality runs the real detection rules over labelled cases and reports, per area:

  • precision: of what JATMP found, how much was right (low precision means false alarms);
  • recall: of what was really there, how much JATMP found (low recall means misses);
  • F1, the balance of the two, and every case the rules got wrong.
Area Rule A case says Counted per families The extractor's families and actors Every family and actor the text names Name indicators The extractor's IPs, domains, URLs and hashes Every indicator an analyst would act on (not benign platforms, private addresses, versions or file names) Value scam The scam rules Whether the item is a scam report Item sectors Critical infrastructure sectors The sectors that are targets Sector geography Target countries The countries that are targets (not the attacker's origin or the hosting country) Country severity Severity Whether the item belongs among the notable items (severity 30 or more) Item

The cases live in tests/quality/<area>.jsonl, one JSON object per line. The first set (0.13) was written by hand from real headlines and from the traps the rules were tuned on: everyday words that are also family names, defanged indicators, smuggling "modus" next to scam "modus", hosting countries. It is small and deliberately hard, so read its numbers as a trend line, not as how JATMP does on your feeds.

docs.title: Corrections become test cases
docs.text:
Export as test cases on the Corrections page (or GET /api/corrections/export.jsonl) turns the active corrections into cases:

  • Not a scam report is a complete label, so it joins the scam area.
  • Wrong entity here and wrong entity everywhere only say what must not be found on those items. They are reported apart: analyst corrections the rules still repeat: 7 of 23. A rule change that brings that number down fixes mistakes analysts actually met.
python manage.py quality --corrections jatmp-corrections.jsonl

Good cases from the export can be copied into tests/quality/ so they guard every later release.

docs.title: The quality gate in CI
docs.text: tests/quality/baseline.json holds the precision and recall of each area when they were last recorded. tests/test_quality.py fails the build when an area falls below it, and lists the cases the rules now get wrong. CI also adds the report to the job summary. When a rule change improves an area, record the new numbers with python manage.py quality --update-baseline and mention them in the changelog ("fraud recall went from 0.706 to 0.82").

docs.title: Enrichment and verdicts
docs.text: This page explains how the indicators found in items get a verdict: which ones are looked up and when, which providers are asked, how their answers are combined, how verdicts age, and what a verdict changes. It also covers the CVE intel refresh, which does the same job for vulnerabilities. The code is in app/processing/enrichment.py, app/intel/clients.py, app/intel/quota.py and app/intel/cve.py.

docs.title: The enrichment run
docs.text:
jobs.run_enrichment runs every enrichment_interval minutes (default 10, minimum 2; the first run is 2 minutes after start-up) and whenever someone clicks Enrich now on the dashboard or Run enrichment batch on the IOC page. It does nothing if automatic enrichment is switched off (Settings → Enrichment) or if no provider has an API key.

Each run only looks up a small, prioritised batch, because the free tiers of most providers allow just a few hundred lookups a day.

docs.title: Which indicators a run picks
docs.text:
With the default enrichment_batch of 8, a run fills its batch in this order:

Tier What it picks In what order 1. Fresh Indicators that have never been looked up and are mentioned in an item published in the last 14 days Highest severity of the items that mention them first, then the most mentioned, then the most recently seen 2. Top-up (only if tier 1 has fewer than 8) Other indicators that have never been looked up: those mentioned in live items, or linked through enrichment (for example a family's indicators pulled from OTX). Indicators that only appear in backfilled items are skipped unless enrich_backfill is on Newest first 3. Re-check (2 extra places) Indicators seen in the last 21 days whose last lookup failed more than 6 hours ago, or came back unknown more than 3 days ago Most mentioned first, then the longest since the last check 4. Aged verdicts (2 extra places) Malicious or suspicious IPs, domains and URLs whose verdict is older than verdict_recheck_days (default 30) and that were mentioned in the last 90 days; see Verdicts that age Oldest verdict first 5. Families (when enrich families is on) Up to 2 of the top 5 trending malware families that haven't been enriched in the last 24 hours By trend score

So a single run handles up to 12 indicators (8 + 2 + 2) and 2 families. Indicators from curated blocklists never wait in this queue: they are marked malicious as soon as they are stored (see Blocklist verdicts).

Each provider works at its own pace. A run first does all its lookups, with one thread per provider working through the indicators that provider supports (enrichment.prefetch). The run therefore takes as long as its slowest provider, rather than the time of all providers added together. The answers are then applied one indicator at a time, and each one is saved as soon as it is done, so a run that fails half-way keeps what it finished. The progress bar shows "lookups" first, then "indicators".

docs.title: The queue
docs.text:
The IOC page (for analysts and admins) and Settings → Enrichment show what the job has in front of it (enrichment.queue_status):

  • how many indicators from the last 14 days are still waiting for their first lookup, and how old the oldest is;
  • how many new indicators arrive per day (averaged over 7 days), compared with what the job can handle per day (batch × runs per day: 8 × 144 = 1,152 with the defaults);
  • how many re-checks and aged verdicts are due.

If more indicators arrive than the job can look up, a note says so.

For each provider with a daily budget, the panel also shows how long the budget lasts at the current pace, and which batch size would spread it over the whole day (quota.pace). For example, VirusTotal's 400 lookups a day last about 8 hours at 8 indicators every 10 minutes. A batch of 2 would spread them across the day, at the cost of a longer queue.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
Every provider with an API key is asked about every type of indicator it supports:

Provider Indicator types Minimum gap between calls Daily budget (default) VirusTotal IP, domain, URL, MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 16 s (vt_min_interval; the free tier allows 4 a minute) 400 (vt_daily_budget; the free tier allows 500) AlienVault OTX IP, domain, URL, MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 — — urlscan.io domain, IP, URL, SHA-256 2 s — ANY.RUN TI Lookup IP, domain, URL, MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 3 s — MalwareBazaar (abuse.ch) MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 1 s — URLhaus (abuse.ch) URL, domain, IP, MD5, SHA-256 1 s — GreyNoise IP 2 s 40 (greynoise_daily_budget) AbuseIPDB IP 1 s 900 (abuseipdb_daily_budget; the free tier allows 1,000)

How the limits work:

  • Gaps between calls are enforced per provider. They keep JATMP within the free tiers' per-minute limits. While one provider waits for its gap, the others carry on. With VirusTotal configured, a full run of 12 indicators still takes about 3 minutes, but the other providers finish their part in the meantime. The gaps are kept in memory, so right after a restart the first call to each provider doesn't wait.
  • Daily budgets are counted per provider and per calendar day on the server (UTC in the Docker image), and they survive restarts. Once a provider's budget is used up, its lookups fail with "daily budget exhausted", the other providers keep working, and the indicator is tried again 6 hours later. You get one notification per provider and day when that happens, for every provider with a budget, including the context providers.
  • The quota panel under Settings → Enrichment shows, for every configured provider with a budget, how many lookups have been used today out of the limit. Analysts and admins see the same figures at the top of the IOC page.
  • A provider error (quota, timeout, HTTP error) never stops the run. It is logged, and the other providers' answers are still used.

docs.title: What a provider's answer contains
docs.text:
Each provider returns its own verdict (malicious, suspicious, clean or unknown), a score, a one-line summary, a link to its page, tags, malware family labels, related indicators, and some raw data. JATMP stores one record per indicator and provider (a later lookup replaces it), and shows them all on the indicator's page.

A few providers need special handling before their answers are combined:

  • OTX says malicious when an indicator appears in 3 or more pulses, or in any pulse that names a family; suspicious for 1–2 pulses; and clean when OTX itself lists the indicator as whitelisted or a known false positive (CDNs and big-tech infrastructure, for example).
  • urlscan.io says malicious when any of up to 20 scans of the indicator was judged malicious, and unknown otherwise.
  • GreyNoise says clean for known benign business services ("RIOT") and benign scanners. Its classification is also shown on the indicator as a badge ("mass scanner", "benign service").

docs.title: Consensus
docs.text:
All the answers from one lookup are combined into the indicator's verdict (_consensus):

  1. Start from the indicator's current verdict (or from nothing, when an aged verdict is being re-checked).
  2. OTX on its own is weak evidence. An OTX malicious without a family name and from fewer than 5 pulses counts as suspicious.
  3. GreyNoise filters out noise. If GreyNoise says an IP is benign, the malicious and suspicious answers of the noisier providers (OTX, AbuseIPDB, urlscan.io) are ignored. Scanners and CDNs turn up in their reports all the time.
  4. The strongest remaining verdict wins: malicious beats suspicious, which beats clean, which beats unknown. One provider saying malicious is enough.
  5. If GreyNoise said benign and no strong provider (VirusTotal, abuse.ch, ANY.RUN) said malicious or suspicious, the verdict is clean.

An analyst's verdict wins. When an analyst has set a verdict on the indicator (✎ Correct on its page; see Corrections and quality), every lookup still stores each provider's answer, but the verdict stays what the analyst said. Marking an indicator not a threat sets it to clean in the same way.

Because the first step starts from the current verdict, a verdict normally only goes up. A later lookup where every provider says unknown won't turn a malicious indicator back. There are two ways down: step 5 (a GreyNoise benign answer turns suspicious or unknown into clean), and the re-check of an aged verdict described next.

Result of the lookup Stored verdict Next lookup At least one provider answered The consensus (unknown if they all said so) If unknown: again after 3 days, as long as the indicator was mentioned in the last 21 days; otherwise not automatically Every provider that was asked failed Unchanged (empty for a first lookup) After 6 hours No provider supports the type, or none answered unknown As for unknown

Enrich now on an indicator's page looks it up again whenever you like (limited per user and per minute, and only one lookup per indicator at a time).

docs.title: Verdicts that age
docs.text:
IPs, domains and URLs change hands. Last year's command-and-control server might host a small online shop today. So every indicator records when its verdict was last given or confirmed, and its page shows "verdict as of date".

Step Rule Setting Re-check A malicious or suspicious IP, domain or URL whose verdict is older than 30 days and that was mentioned in the last 90 days is looked up again (tier 4 above). The new answer replaces the old verdict, even when it is lower. The items that mention the indicator then get the bonus of their strongest remaining indicator, or none verdict_recheck_days (0 = never) Leave the feeds Once the verdict is older than 60 days without being confirmed again, the indicator is left out of the IOC export feeds (txt, csv, json) and TAXII. STIX indicators carry valid_until = verdict date + 60 days. The pages and the REST API still list it: the pages mark it aged, and the API includes its verdict_at verdict_feed_days (0 = keep it in the feeds) Confirmed again Any lookup that gets an answer, or a blocklist that lists the indicator again (ScamSniffer, for example), resets the verdict date to today. That includes an analyst's verdict, so it doesn't age out of the feeds while the indicator is still being mentioned —

File hashes never age: a file is always the same file.

docs.title: What a verdict changes
docs.text:
When a lookup finishes:

Effect When Family attribution. Up to 5 family labels per provider (such as trojan.lumma/lummastealer or Win32/Formbook) are matched to a known family, skipping generic words (trojan, generic, win32, agent, android…), legitimate tools and platforms. The indicator is linked to the family as attributed-to, so a hash posted on Bluesky connects to every article about that family Always Related indicators. Up to 8 per provider (a domain's IPs, a URL's host) are created and linked as related Always Severity goes up. Every item that mentions the indicator gets +12 (malicious) or +5 (suspicious), replacing any earlier indicator confirmed reason; see Severity scoring The verdict went up Severity goes down. Each item that mentions the indicator gets the bonus of its strongest remaining indicator, or loses the bonus The verdict went down (an aged verdict re-checked, or an analyst lowered it) Webhook ioc.malicious The verdict turned malicious (through the providers or an analyst), and the indicator may be shared Context lookup (Shodan, Censys…) The verdict turned malicious and run context lookups when an indicator turns malicious is on Hosting country of an IP: taken from the offline GeoIP database first, otherwise from IPinfo, Censys, Shodan, VirusTotal, AbuseIPDB, CrowdSec or OTX, in that order IP indicators

docs.title: Family enrichment
docs.text:
For a trending malware family (tier 5 above, or Enrich on a family's page), JATMP looks for fresh indicators:

  • OTX pulse search for the family's name. Short or ambiguous names such as "Play" are searched as "Play" ransomware. OTX's search is fuzzy, so only pulses that really name the family in their title, tags or family list are used. Up to 40 indicators from each of the first 5 pulses are linked to the family.
  • ANY.RUN TI Lookup for threatName:"<family>" over the last 14 days: the sandbox tasks and up to 40 related IOCs.

These indicators are new and have never been looked up, so later runs pick them up in tier 2.

docs.title: Context lookups
docs.text: Context lookup on an IP, domain or hash asks the infrastructure providers (Shodan or its keyless InternetDB, Censys, CrowdSec CTI, Pulsedive, Hybrid Analysis and IPinfo) about open ports, services, network owner, reputation and sandbox results. They are never part of the scheduled run, because their free tiers are small. Each provider has its own daily budget (context_daily_budget, default 100), and manual lookups are limited per user and per minute. The answers are stored like any other enrichment, so their verdicts count towards the consensus too.

docs.title: CVE intel
docs.text:
CVEs are enriched by a separate job, jobs.run_cve_intel, every 6 hours (the first run is 3 minutes after start-up) and whenever someone clicks Refresh CVE intel. Switching the setting off only stops the scheduled run; you can still refresh by hand.

  1. Pick up to 60 CVEs mentioned in the last 30 days that haven't been checked in the last 24 hours: never-checked ones first, then the most recently mentioned.
  2. CISA KEV. The catalogue is downloaded and cached for 12 hours (data/cache/cisa_kev.json). A CVE in the catalogue gets its KEV entry (date added, due date, known ransomware use, vendor, product). A CVE that isn't in it gets an empty entry, so a CVE removed from KEV loses its badge. If the catalogue can't be downloaded, the existing KEV data is kept.
  3. FIRST EPSS. One request per 80 CVEs gives the probability of exploitation within the next 30 days and its percentile.
  4. NVD CVSS. One request per CVE, but only when its CVSS score is missing or more than 7 days old. Without an NVD key, that is at most 10 per run, 6.5 seconds apart; with a key, 50 per run, 0.8 seconds apart. Two failures in a row stop the NVD lookups for the rest of the run ("NVD unavailable, CVSS retried next run").
  5. The results are stored on the CVE and saved every 10 CVEs.

KEV, EPSS and CVSS feed the CVE list, the CVEs by exploitation risk chart and the ranking of trending CVEs. See CVE priority.

docs.title: Housekeeping and re-analysis
docs.text: This page covers the processes that keep the database small and consistent over time: the nightly clean-up, the retention tiers, the removal of personal data, the one-off jobs that apply new rules to stored items, and what happens when JATMP restarts. The code is in app/jobs.py.

docs.title: Nightly housekeeping
docs.text:
run_housekeeping runs every day at 03:30 by default. You can change the time and the time zone under Settings → General (housekeeping_time and schedule_timezone); the default time zone is UTC. It works through these steps in order:

# Step Default Setting 1 Delete job run records started more than 30 days ago Always — 2 Delete notifications older than 30 days Always — 3 Slim items published more than 180 days ago (see below), up to 20,000 a night On retention_full_days (0 = never) 4 Delete webhook deliveries older than 30 days Always — 5 Delete items published more than N days ago, then recount mentions and remove indicators nothing refers to any more Off retention_days (0 = keep forever) 6 Delete AI answers (questions and answers) older than 90 days Always — 7 Prune scammer identifiers that haven't been mentioned for 365 days On fraud_identifier_days (0 = keep)

docs.title: Slimming
docs.text:
Once an item is older than retention_full_days, it keeps everything that analysis and statistics need and loses the bulk:

Kept Changed Title, link, source, dates, kind, tags The text is cut to its first 400 characters (at a word boundary, ending with " …") All entity links, the severity and its reasons, the fraud score and its reasons The provider data keeps only short simple values (TLP, sector, country…); lists and long texts are removed Geography, sectors, the AI summary The item is marked as slimmed. Its page says the text was trimmed and links to the original

The search index updates itself automatically. Slimming is saved every 1,000 items, so on an old installation where you have just switched it on, the first run is spread over several nights. python manage.py slim does it all at once.

Since the full text is gone, any later re-analysis of a slimmed item (a re-score, or a rules change) works on the snippet and may find less. Geography keeps the countries the feed provided when the item was collected, because those aren't in the snippet.

docs.title: Deleting old items
docs.text:
This is off by default. When you set retention_days, items published before the cut-off are deleted, together with their entity links and geography. After that:

  • every entity's mention count is recalculated from the links that remain;
  • indicators (hashes, IPs, domains, URLs) with no mentions and no enrichment links are deleted;
  • families, actors, CVEs, scam types, brands and sectors are kept as history, even when nothing mentions them any more.

The database file doesn't shrink by itself after a large deletion. Run python manage.py vacuum to give the space back.

docs.title: Scammer identifiers (UU PDP)
docs.text: Phone numbers, bank accounts and e-wallets whose last mention is older than fraud_identifier_days (365 by default) are deleted, together with their links. The last mention is the publication date of the latest item that names the identifier, so an identifier that keeps being reported is kept. Crypto wallets are not personal data and are always kept. See Scams and fraud.

docs.title: Re-analysis of stored items
docs.text:
Detection and scoring rules improve from one version to the next. Without re-analysis, items stored by an older version would keep their old results, and the dashboards would compare items judged by different rules. So each analysis has a rules version:

  1. The code holds a version number for the rules (for example fraud.RULES_VERSION = 6).
  2. The database remembers which version the stored items were analysed with (here, the setting fraud_version).
  3. A few seconds after every start-up, a one-off job compares the two. If they match, it does nothing. If they don't, it re-analyses every stored item and then records the new version.
Job Starts after Rules version What it redoes run_content_cleanup 15 s content_version Removes text that newer cleaning rules strip out (stylesheet rules inside posts), then re-runs the scam and sector analysis for the items that changed run_geotag 20 s geo_version Language, source country, target countries and provinces for every item, and the hosting country of every IP from the GeoIP database run_dedup 30 s dedup_version The fingerprints of every article, oldest first, so the first outlet to publish a story stays the original. On every start it also repairs any article marked as a copy of itself, so it reappears in the feed as an original run_fraudtag 40 s fraud_version Scam types, brands, identifiers, losses, victims and the fraud score of every item, oldest first (so the spreading check sees the earlier reports) run_sectortag 60 s sector_version The critical infrastructure sectors of every item run_digesttag 75 s digest_version Item.is_digest of every item (newsletters and round-ups). Also manage.py digesttag, after changing a source's "digest" setting run_rescore_if_outdated 90 s severity_version The severity of every item, from its text and linked entities, keeping the enrichment bonus and the last AI assessment (the same as Re-score all items). It runs last, so it sees the entities the jobs above have settled

These jobs work through the items in chunks of 500 (200 for the content clean-up), save after each chunk, and show their progress in the job status. Their staggered start times keep them from competing with each other, or with the first collection runs, for the database. They also respect analysts' corrections: an item marked not a scam report keeps a fraud score of 0, and severity is computed only from the links analysts left in place (see Corrections and quality).

Before a rules change ships, python manage.py quality measures it against the labelled cases in tests/quality/, and CI refuses a change that makes any area worse (see Measuring the rules).

You can also run some of them by hand. Geography, fraud and sectors have manage.py geotag, fraudtag and sectortag; geography and the scam analysis can also be started from the interface (Settings, and Re-analyse items on the scam & fraud dashboard), and finish with a notification. Severity has Re-score all items and manage.py rescore. The content clean-up and dedup jobs only run after an upgrade.

Entity extraction has no rules version. Re-extracting rebuilds every link, which is expensive and changes mention counts that analysts may rely on, so it only happens when you ask for it:

Tool What it does Notes Re-score all items (Settings), manage.py rescore Recalculates severity from the stored text and the linked entities Keeps the indicator confirmed bonus and the last AI assessment. No network calls manage.py reextract Deletes the regex, kb and heuristic links and extracts everything again; re-scores severity; re-runs the scam and sector analysis; recounts mentions; removes families and actors left with no mentions or links Keeps feed and llm links, the enrichment bonus, the last AI assessment and every analyst correction (removed links stay removed). Run it after an upgrade that changes the extraction rules, as the upgrade notes say. It extracts from the stored text, so entities found in the full text of an item that retention has since trimmed are not found again: back up first, and prefer ioc-clean when only the IP / SHA-1 rules changed manage.py ioc-clean [--apply] Looks only at regex links of IP and SHA-1 indicators and removes a link when the value is still in the item's text but the current extractor no longer produces it (version numbers, git commits); recounts mentions; deletes an indicator left with no links. A dry run unless --apply is given Never touches feed, llm, kb or analyst links, nor links whose value is not in the stored text (trimmed items)

See Severity scoring.

docs.title: Monthly GeoIP update
docs.text: When update the GeoIP database automatically is on, run_geoip_update downloads a fresh offline database (DB-IP Lite, or MaxMind GeoLite2 if you have a license key) at 04:00 UTC on the 5th of every month. It then re-runs geo-tagging, so the hosting countries of IPs reflect the new data.

docs.title: Start-up and restarts
docs.text:
At start-up (see Architecture), JATMP creates any missing tables and columns, adds built-in sources that a newer version introduced, encrypts secrets that an older version stored in plain text, marks every run that was still queued or running as aborted, schedules the jobs, starts the scheduler, and rebuilds the AI auto-summary queue.

Some state lives only in memory, so a restart resets it:

State What a restart does Progress of running jobs The runs are marked aborted. Start them again if you need to AI auto-summary queue Rebuilt from the live items of the last 24 hours that qualify (severity 40 or more, no summary, not a copy) Trend cache (45 s), settings cache (5 s) and the cache of active corrections (30 s) Rebuilt on the next request Gaps between provider calls, API-key rate windows, per-user action limits Start afresh

Everything else is in the database and survives a restart: every item, entity and verdict (with its date), the providers' daily budgets, queued webhook deliveries (sent on the next 30-second tick), the rules versions, analysts' corrections, notifications and the run history.

docs.title: Ingest and analysis
docs.text:
This page follows each entry a collector returns, from the question "have we seen this before?" to a stored item that is scored, linked to its entities and tagged with its geography. All of it happens inside the collection run, in one database transaction per batch (pipeline.ingest_committed), so you never see an item that is only half analysed.

The entries arrive here already filtered: if the source has a topic filter, the entries it dropped never reach the pipeline (see Topic filters). Analysts' corrections are respected throughout, so a link an analyst removed or an item marked not a scam report stays that way (see Corrections and quality).

docs.title: The ten steps
docs.text:
For every entry in a batch, pipeline.ingest() runs these steps in order:

# Step What it stores on the item Code 1 Skip entries already stored — ingest 2 Clean the text and apply limits Title, text, link, tags, provider data, TLP, publication date strip_html, safe_url, _slim_raw 3 Spot copies from other outlets, and newsletters Fingerprint, which item it copies, whether it is a newsletter or round-up fingerprint, find_original, digest.is_digest 4 Extract entities (the entities, linked in step 8) extractor.extract_all, tag_families 5 Score severity Severity and its reasons severity.score_item 6 Analyse for scams and fraud Fraud score, reasons, losses, victims fraud.apply 7 Tag critical infrastructure sectors (sector entities) sectors.apply 8 Link the entities One link per entity; entity counters link_entities 9 Record blocklist verdicts Enrichment records and verdicts mark_listed 10 Work out the geography Language, source country, target countries and provinces geo.tag_item

The order matters in two places:

  • Severity (step 5) is scored before the fraud and sector entities exist (steps 6 and 7). Scam types, brands, scammer identifiers and sectors therefore never add severity points. A scam report gets its own fraud score instead, and the two scores stay independent on purpose.
  • Sectors (step 7) come after fraud (step 6), because a scam that mentions a bank is usually not an attack on the finance sector (see the rule below).

Once the whole batch is processed, the transaction is committed and the trend cache is cleared. Occasionally another run stores one of the same entries at the same moment (a scheduled run and a backfill of the same source, for example). The database's uniqueness check then fails, so JATMP rolls the batch back and tries again, up to three times, skipping whatever the other run already stored.

docs.title: 1. New or already stored?
docs.text:
An entry is identified by its source and external id. The external id is the provider's own id for the entry (an RSS GUID, a post URI, a pulse id), or failing that its URL, or failing that its title. Ids longer than 500 characters (URLs with tracking parameters, typically) keep their first 434 characters followed by #sha256:<hash of the whole id>, so two long ids that only differ at the end never get mixed up.

The ids of a whole batch are checked with one database query per 500 ids. If the same id appears twice in one batch, it is stored once.

Entries that grow. ThreatFox is a special case: it delivers one entry per malware family and day, and new IOCs for that day keep arriving. When such an entry is already stored, its new indicators are added to the existing item, its title is updated with the new count, and it is scored again (keeping any enrichment bonus and AI assessment). Every other kind of known entry is simply skipped.

The same story published by another source is not a duplicate at this step. It is stored, and step 3 decides whether it is a copy.

docs.title: 2. Cleaning and limits
docs.text:
Feed content comes from outside, so it is treated as untrusted. Before anything else reads it:

Field What happens Text For articles, <script> and <style> blocks and all HTML tags are removed, HTML entities are decoded, stylesheet rules that some blog plugins print into the text are removed, and whitespace is tidied up. Posts, pulses and scans are already plain text. The text is cut at 50,000 characters Link Only kept if it starts with http:// or https:// and contains no line breaks, so a javascript: link can never reach a page. Up to 2,000 characters Title, author Cut at 1,000 and 250 characters Tags At most 50, each up to 80 characters Publication date Taken from the provider. If it is missing, JATMP uses the current time. If it is in the future, JATMP also uses the current time (clocks drift, and some feeds post-date entries) Provider data Kept small: text values over 2,000 characters, or identical to the item's text, are dropped TLP The entry's own TLP if the feed gives one (OTX, MISP), normalised to CLEAR, GREEN, AMBER or RED Origin live for scheduled and manual collection, backfill for history

The cleaning patterns are written to run in linear time, even on hostile input. Every article passes through them, and a pattern that got stuck backtracking would tie up a scheduler thread that can't be stopped.

docs.title: 3. Cross-source duplicates
docs.text:
News gets syndicated: the same wire story can appear on five Indonesian news sites within a few hours. If each copy counted separately, everything in that story would look as if it were trending. So JATMP gives every article a fingerprint:

  1. Take the title and remove an outlet suffix such as " - ANTARA News" or " | Republika Online".
  2. Lower-case it and keep only the words.
  3. If the title has fewer than 5 words (for example "Weekly update"), add up to 30 words from the first 400 characters of the text.
  4. If there are still fewer than 6 words, give up: there is too little to compare.
  5. Otherwise, hash the words.

JATMP then looks for an article from another source with the same fingerprint, published within 4 days before or after this one. If it finds one, the new item becomes a copy that points to the original: the earliest item, never another copy, and never the item itself. Items in the same batch are compared with each other as well.

Copies are stored like any other item, and you can see them in the interface:

  • The feed lists each story once and says how many copies it hid; tick Show copies to list them, marked with a copy badge.
  • The item page and the preview say "Copy of original" on a copy, and "Also carried by N other outlets" on the original.

Every count of stories (the dashboards, trend scores, the scam spreading check, the executive summary and the reports) counts a story and its copies once. Only per-outlet figures, such as Items per source, count each copy for the outlet that published it. See Counting rules. Posts, pulses and scans are not fingerprinted.

Newsletters and round-ups. In the same step, every item (not only articles) is checked for being a digest: a newsletter, weekly round-up or podcast that wraps several unrelated stories in one post, such as Cisco Talos' Threat Source. The answer is stored as items.is_digest. A digest is still a normal item everywhere (feed, counts, severity), but what it mentions side by side is not evidence that those things belong together, so co-mentions skip it and correlation discounts it. How it is recognised is described under Correlation.

docs.title: 4. Entity extraction
docs.text: JATMP scans the title, the text and the tags together. Extraction has four parts.

docs.title: Indicators, CVEs and techniques (origin regex)
docs.text:
First, the text is refanged: the usual ways of writing indicators safely are turned back into the real thing. hxxp(s) becomes http(s), fxp becomes ftp, [.] (.) {.} [dot] (dot) and \. become ., [:] becomes :, [://] becomes ://, [/] becomes /, and [at] becomes @.

Type Pattern Rejected when cve CVE-YYYY-NNNN… — technique T1xxx or T1xxx.yyy — sha256, sha1, md5 64, 40 or 32 hex characters It is part of a longer hash that was already found; it has fewer than 6 different characters (000000…); it sits inside a URL (right after / = # - _ or right before / - _); or an MD5 / SHA-1 sits in a token containing utm_, token=, session, /commit/, /blob/ and the like; or a SHA-1 follows at, commit, rev, revision or sha (a git commit, as in "file.py at 4fbffbc6…") ip IPv4 address It isn't public (private, loopback, reserved, multicast, link-local); it is a well-known public DNS resolver (8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1, 9.9.9.9…); it follows the word version, build, release, firmware, v, Chrome, Windows, kernel and the like (so it is really a version number; "server 91.92.243.10" is not); it is part of an advisory's version list (versions prior to 6.14.105.0, up to 1.5.1.6, 12.1.0.0 through 12.1.1.2, builds include 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1), and then it is dropped everywhere in that text; it is followed by .digit (as in 1.2.3.4.5); or it comes right after a . url http(s)://… Its host is a benign domain; it is just the front page of a paste or file-sharing service; or, in strict mode, it wasn't written defanged domain Host names with a 2–24 letter top-level domain It, or a domain above it, is benign; its "top-level domain" is really a file extension (.exe, .zip, .php, .json…); it is an IP; or, in strict mode, it was neither defanged nor the host of a URL that was kept

Strict mode. News and social sources (every category except intel) are read in strict mode, where a domain or URL only counts if the author defanged it (or it is the host of a defanged URL). Ordinary links in an article, such as the vendor's blog or a reference, are almost never indicators. When a researcher writes evil[.]com, on the other hand, they mean it. Intel sources are read without strict mode, because everything they publish is meant as an indicator. IPs and hashes are picked up in both modes.

Benign domains. About 200 domains are never treated as indicators: platforms, search engines, social networks, link shorteners, security media and vendors, standards bodies, and Indonesian media, banks and government sites (for example bleepingcomputer.com, cisa.gov, t.me, detik.com, bssn.go.id). Their subdomains are benign too.

Abused hosting services. Paste, file-sharing and code-hosting services (Pastebin, GitHub and its raw content, Google Drive, Dropbox, MEGA, Discord's CDN, transfer.sh and about 20 more) are legitimate, so their domain is never an indicator. A URL on them that points somewhere (a paste, a release asset, a shared file) is one: in an item that quotes hxxps://pastebin[.]com/raw/abcd1234, the URL is kept and pastebin.com is not.

docs.title: Known families and actors (origin kb)
docs.text:
The knowledge base (app/knowledge.py, plus any additions you make in data/knowledge_extra.json) holds about 150 malware families and 45 threat actors, with their aliases. Every match becomes an entity with the official name and the family's category (ransomware, stealer, loader and so on).

Some names are also everyday words, or are four letters or shorter ("Play", "Fog", "Hook", "Conti"). These only count next to a qualifier: "Play ransomware", "the Fog group", "malware called Hook". The exception is a name written in its own distinctive spelling, with a capital in the middle or a digit inside the word ("RedLine", "Cl0p", "SafePay"): that spelling is no everyday word, so it counts on its own, while "redline" or "Safepay checkout" still don't. Ambiguous actor names likewise need a word such as APT, group or threat actor within two words of the name ("Bitter APT").

docs.title: New family names (origin heuristic)
docs.text:
Families that aren't in the knowledge base yet are exactly the ones that matter for spotting new campaigns. So the extractor also looks for a name right next to a malware noun:

  • In English: "Zorblax ransomware", "the PipeMagic backdoor". The nouns are ransomware, infostealer, stealer, loader, botnet, backdoor, trojan, wiper, rootkit, malware, spyware, dropper, keylogger and RAT.
  • In Indonesian, where the noun comes first: "ransomware Brain Cipher", "malware bernama Lumma", "trojan perbankan Mamont". These patterns run when the text is in Indonesian or its language is unclear.

To keep false positives down, a candidate must pass every one of these checks:

  1. It is a single word, without a hyphen. (Multi-word family names belong in the knowledge base.)
  2. In a headline written in title case ("WhiteArmor Ransomware Demands…"), the name must be CamelCase or mix letters and digits. In ordinary sentences, a capitalised word is enough, unless it starts the sentence.
  3. It isn't a generic word (new, Android, Russian, sophisticated, AI…), a legitimate tool that attackers misuse (AnyDesk, ConnectWise, PsExec, Mimikatz…), a platform (Facebook, Telegram, Shopee…), a country or nationality, or a short all-capitals acronym.
  4. It wasn't already found in the same text.

If the name turns out to be a known alias, it is mapped to the knowledge-base family instead. A heuristic family scores less than a known one (6 severity points instead of 10), and it only trends once two sources name it.

docs.title: What the feed delivers (origin feed)
docs.text:
• Structured indicators that a collector attaches (OTX pulse indicators, urlscan scan URLs, ThreatFox IOCs, MISP attributes, ScamSniffer domains) are added exactly as delivered.
  • Tags on intel sources that name a known family (OTX's malware families, ThreatFox family names) become family entities. Tags on news and social sources are free-form and are ignored here. A tag of three characters or fewer, or an everyday word, is never treated as a family.

Finally, all findings are de-duplicated by type and value.

docs.title: 5. Severity
docs.text: The text and the entities from step 4 give the item its severity from 0 to 100, along with the list of reasons shown on the item page. The rules, weights and dampeners have their own page: Severity scoring.

docs.title: 6. Scam and fraud analysis
docs.text: The same text is then read a second time, as a possible scam report. JATMP looks for scam types, impersonated brands, reported losses and victims, and scammer identifiers. Identifiers are only taken from items that are about a scam, and only where the sentence makes clear they belong to the scammer. The result is the fraud score. A fraud score above 0 is what makes an item a scam report, everywhere in JATMP. To keep this fast, the "spreading" counts for each scam type are worked out once per scam type and day for the whole batch. If an analyst has marked the item not a scam report, the analysis is skipped and the fraud score stays 0, also when the scam rules change and stored items are re-analysed. The rules and points are on Scams and fraud.

docs.title: 7. Critical infrastructure sectors
docs.text:
Each sector defined by Perpres 82/2022 (government administration, energy & mineral resources, transportation, finance, health, ICT, food, defence) has an English and Indonesian vocabulary describing the organisations and services in it. Each sector collects points:

Signal Points Each match in the title 2 Each match in the body (first 20,000 characters) 1, up to 4 per sector The feed states the sector (ransomware.live victim sector, OTX industries) 3

A sector is tagged when it reaches 2 points, with three exceptions:

  • One word in the title, and nothing else. If there is no match in the body and the feed doesn't state the sector, a title word needs 3 points, unless the title names exactly one sector and describes an attack on it ("Serangan ransomware lumpuhkan layanan rumah sakit"). "Hospital food vendor hit by phishing" is therefore not a health-sector item.
  • Scams and finance. For a scam report, finance only counts if the feed says so or the text describes an attack (a breach, a hack, dibobol, a leak and so on). Most scams only mention a bank as the way money was paid.
  • Round-ups and newsletters are judged on their title alone.

An item gets at most 3 sectors, strongest first. Sectors are stored as entities of type sector.

docs.title: 8. Linking entities
docs.text:
Everything found in steps 4, 6 and 7 is now linked to the item:

  1. Existing entities are looked up with one query per entity type (per 500 values), and the missing ones are created together. A blocklist item with 500 domains therefore costs two queries, not 500.
  2. A new IP gets its hosting country from the offline GeoIP database straight away, if one is installed.
  3. Each entity gets one link to the item, recording how it was found (regex, kb, heuristic, feed). Links that an analyst removed are skipped: the entity on this item for wrong entity here, and on every item for wrong entity everywhere or not a threat. The same check applies when entities are re-extracted, added by the AI or merged into a ThreatFox item.
  4. The entity's mention count goes up by one. Its first-seen and last-seen dates move to the item's publication date if that is earlier or later (so a backfill can move first-seen back in time). If the entity had no category yet, it gets one.

docs.title: 9. Blocklist verdicts
docs.text: Some sources are curated blocklists, where everything listed is malicious by definition (ScamSniffer's wallet-drainer domains, for example). Their items carry a "listed by" marker. Every structured indicator on such an item gets an enrichment record from that list with the verdict malicious, and indicators that were never looked up get the verdict malicious straight away. They skip the enrichment queue and use no provider quota. When the list names an indicator again on a later day, its verdict date is refreshed, so the verdict doesn't age (see Verdicts that age).

docs.title: Language and source country
docs.text:
The language is decided by counting common words in the first 4,000 characters. With at least 6 words, the text is id (Indonesian) if it has at least 3 Indonesian common words and 20% more of them than English ones, and en if it has at least 3 English common words and no fewer than Indonesian ones. Otherwise the language is left empty and the source's configured language is used instead.

The source country is the country configured for the source, or Indonesia for an item written in Indonesian.

docs.title: Target countries and provinces
docs.text:
Target countries are where the victims are or where the activity takes place. Each country collects points:

Signal Points The country's name in the title 2 The country's name in the body 1 for the first mention, 0.5 for the 2nd to 5th, then nothing … when it is a nationality ("Indonesian", "Russian") × 0.75 … when a target word comes right before it ("against", "in", "targeting", "di", "menyerang"…) × 1.5 An Indonesian province, city, regency or institution (BSSN, OJK, Pertamina…) Indonesia gets +3 in the title or +2 in the body; the province gets +2 or +1 An ambiguous Indonesian place name after Kota, Kabupaten, Pemkot and the like ("Kota Malang") As above Weak Indonesian acronyms (BCA, KPU…) Only count in Indonesian text, or when Indonesia already has 1.5 points .go.id, .co.id and .ac.id domains in the text Indonesia gets +2 for each, up to +4 Leak-site postings in the form victim.com (GB) That country gets +3 Countries stated by the feed (ransomware.live victim country, OTX targeted countries) +10 each

A country becomes a target with 1.5 points or more (countries stated by the feed always qualify), up to 4 per item. Provinces need 1 point, up to 4, and only count when Indonesia is a target.

Attackers are not targets. When a country is named as the origin of the attacker, it is set aside: "Russian hackers", "China-nexus", "Iran-linked", "attributed to North Korea", "peretas asal Rusia". Neither are the places where criminals trade or servers sit (0.13.1): "sold on Russian forums", "Chinese-language marketplaces", "hosted in the Netherlands", "a Dutch hosting provider", "server di Singapura". Likewise, "Latin America" doesn't mean the US. Names that only make sense in Indonesian text are ignored elsewhere, and a headline written in capitals is converted to title case first so that names can be recognised.

Each target is stored with its country, its province if any, its score, and whether it came from the text or the feed. The hosting country of an IP is a different thing. It is stored on the indicator itself (from GeoIP when the indicator is created, and from the providers during enrichment) and never counts as a target.

docs.title: The National (Indonesia) view
docs.text: The National (ID) switch keeps the items that target Indonesia, plus items from Indonesian outlets that name no other target country. Everything else counts as international. Every list, chart, statistic, report and the IOC table apply the same condition.

docs.title: Severity scoring
docs.text:
Every item gets a severity from 0 to 100 when it is stored, together with the list of reasons behind it. You can see the breakdown by clicking the score on the item page. This page lists every rule; the code is in app/processing/severity.py.

Severity is a triage aid. It answers the question "how urgently should an analyst read this?" It is not a CVSS score and not a probability. Scam reports have their own fraud score, and the two are never added together.

docs.title: How the score is built
docs.text:
severity = text signals            (4 groups: the strongest term, plus half the runner-up, in each group)
         + entity signals          (family, actor, CVEs, indicators, techniques)
         + structured-intel base   (pulses, analyses, scans)
         × dampeners               (patch note ×0.7, round-up / non-incident ×0.5)
         → cap for routine leak-site posts (35)
         → rounded, kept between 0 and 100

After that, two things can still raise a stored score: an indicator that enrichment confirms as malicious, and the AI assessment. See After ingest.

docs.title: Text signals
docs.text:
The title, the first 20,000 characters of the text, and the tags are matched against four signal groups. The terms within one group are different ways of saying the same kind of thing, so they must not all add up:

  • Only the strongest term in a group counts in full. The runner-up counts at half weight, and anything after that is ignored.
  • A term that appears in the title counts 1.5 times, because headlines name the real subject while the body mentions everything in passing. Not in the title of a roundup, a guide or other non-incident content: such a title lists topics, it isn't about them.
  • An English term and its Indonesian equivalent share a label and count once.
  • The contributions of the different groups are added together.

docs.title: Exploitation
docs.text:
Signal Points Examples of what matches zero-day 30 zero-day, 0-day exploited in the wild 30 actively exploited, in the wild, under active attack, mass exploitation, sedang / aktif dieksploitasi listed in CISA KEV 28 KEV, known exploited vulnerability public exploit code 18 PoC released, exploit code published exploitation mentioned 10 exploit, exploited, exploiting, eksploitasi

When the strongest exploitation term is worth 18 points or more (including the title bonus), the item counts as actively exploited. The patch-note dampener below then no longer applies, because a bug that is being exploited is still urgent even when a patch is available.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: Signal Points Examples of what matches remote code execution 14 RCE, unauthenticated attacker, pre-auth, eksekusi kode jarak jauh destructive / wiper 14 wiper, destructive malware, data-destroying critical / CVSS ≥ 9 12 CVSS 9.8, "critical flaw", "rated critical", celah kritis (but not "critical infrastructure") authentication bypass 12 auth bypass, bypasses authentication service disruption 10 halts production or operations, shuts down plants or systems, disrupts operations, systems went offline, layanan lumpuh, sistem lumpuh, data terenkripsi privilege escalation 6 privilege escalation, LPE, EoP high severity 6 high-severity
