docs.title: Entity signals
docs.text:
The entities the extractor found are evidence in their own right. Each kind counts once:

Signal Points A known malware family (from the knowledge base, a feed or a provider) 10 Only an unknown family, found by the "Name ransomware" pattern 6 A known threat actor 8 CVEs 5 for the first, +2 for each additional CVE, up to 11 Indicators (IPs, domains, URLs, hashes) 8, or 12 with five or more ATT&CK technique ids 3 The item is a pulse or analysis / a scan (structured intel) 6 / 4

Scam types, brands, scammer identifiers and sectors add no severity points (see the order of the ingest steps).

docs.title: Dampeners and caps
docs.text:
These are applied after everything above has been added up, in this order. Apart from the leak-site cap, they only look at the title:

Rule Effect Triggered by Patch or advisory × 0.7 "fixes", "patches", "Patch Tuesday", "security update", "addresses", "hotfix", tambal, pembaruan keamanan… — unless the item is actively exploited (see above) Round-up, guide or non-incident × 0.5 "week in review", "roundup", "top 10", "how to", "what is", webinar, podcast, survey, "announces", funding, acquisition, training, tips; outages, pricing, lawsuits, GDPR; cara mengatasi, begini cara, kenali, apa itu, seminar, peluncuran, promo, diskon Routine leak-site posting capped at 35 A post saying a group "added / claims / listed … victims / leak site". Ransomware trackers publish hundreds of these every day

Both multipliers can apply to the same item (× 0.35 in total). The result is rounded and kept between 0 and 100. Each reduction appears in the breakdown as a reason with negative points, so the reasons always add up to the score (allowing for rounding).

docs.title: Worked examples
docs.text:
All three were calculated by running the text through score_item.

1. An exploited zero-day. "LockBit ransomware exploits Citrix zero-day to hit Indonesian hospitals", with a body describing an actively exploited RCE, one CVE, one technique and three defanged indicators:

Reason Points How zero-day 45 30, in the title × 1.5; the strongest exploitation term exploited in the wild 15 30 × 0.5 as the runner-up in exploitation remote code execution 14 The strongest impact term ransomware 18 12, in the title × 1.5; the strongest threat class term active campaign 10 The strongest activity term sensitive sector 4 5 × 1.5 (hospitals, in the title) × 0.5 as the runner-up known malware family 10 LockBit 1 CVE(s) 5 3 indicator(s) 8 ATT&CK techniques 3 Total 132 → 100 Capped

2. A patch note. "Microsoft fixes critical Exchange flaw in Patch Tuesday update", with a body mentioning one CVE and remote code execution:

Reason Points How critical / CVSS ≥ 9 18 12, in the title × 1.5; the strongest impact term remote code execution 7 14 × 0.5 as the runner-up in impact 1 CVE(s) 5 patch / advisory only −9 (18 + 7 + 5) × 0.7 = 21. There is no exploitation signal, so the dampener applies Total 21

If the body had also said "exploited in the wild", the item would have scored 65 with no dampener: exploited in the wild 30, exploitation mentioned 5 (10 × 0.5 as the runner-up, from the word "exploited"), and then 18 + 7 + 5 as before.

3. A scam warning. "Waspada penipuan APK undangan pernikahan mengatasnamakan BRI, korban rugi Rp 1,2 miliar" scores a severity of only 9 (penipuan in the title: phishing / social engineering, 6 × 1.5). The same item has a fraud score of 83: malicious APK lure 28, also impersonation 4, impersonates BRI 10, losses of Rp 1.2 billion 15, 120 victims 10, scammer identifiers 8, and a police warning 8. That is intended. As a cyber threat it is minor, but as a scam report it is serious, and it ranks high on the scam & fraud dashboard.

docs.title: After ingest
docs.text:
Event Effect on the stored score Reason shown One of the item's indicators turns malicious in enrichment +12 indicator confirmed malicious (ip) One of the item's indicators turns suspicious +5. If it later turns malicious, the score rises by another 7 and the reason shows +12 indicator confirmed suspicious (…) A malicious or suspicious indicator is re-checked and its verdict goes down The item keeps the bonus of its strongest remaining indicator, or loses it Updated, or removed An analyst sets an indicator's verdict The bonus follows the analyst's verdict, up or down Updated, or removed An analyst removes an entity from the item (wrong entity here, wrong entity everywhere, not a threat) The item is re-scored from the links that remain, keeping the enrichment bonus and the AI assessment The entity's reason disappears The AI rates the item higher than the rule-based score The score is raised towards the AI's number, by at most +20. It never goes below the rule-based score AI assessment (capped), with an AI badge

Each item keeps only one indicator confirmed reason, for its strongest verdict, so several malicious indicators don't add +12 each. The AI assessment is replaced rather than added to when an item is analysed again: its old points are taken off first, so a lower new assessment can remove them. Both adjustments are capped at 100.

docs.title: Recomputing scores
docs.text:
When the terms, weights or dampeners change in a new version, the rules version (severity.RULES_VERSION) goes up, and every stored item is re-scored once, about 90 seconds after the new version first starts (jobs.run_rescore_if_outdated). That way old and new items are scored by the same rules before the trends compare them. You can also re-score by hand:

Tool What it starts from Keeps the enrichment bonus Keeps the AI assessment Re-score all items (Settings), manage.py rescore The stored text and the entities already linked (with how they were found). Nothing is re-extracted and no network calls are made Yes Yes manage.py reextract A fresh extraction of the stored text, which rebuilds the regex, kb and heuristic links (except those analysts removed) and the scam and sector analysis Yes Yes

In every case, the points that don't come from the text are added back afterwards (severity.carry_over): the indicator confirmed bonus for the strongest verdict among the item's indicators today, and the last AI assessment. The AI assessment remembers the severity the model proposed, so it is applied again to the new score with the same cap. If the new score already reaches the model's number, it adds nothing. AI assessments stored before version 0.11 don't have a proposed severity, so they keep their original points.

Slimmed items (past the full-text retention period) are re-scored from their snippet, so their score may drop. See Housekeeping and re-analysis.

docs.title: Reading a score
docs.text:
Range Typical content 80–100 Exploited zero-days, supply-chain compromises, ransomware campaigns with indicators 50–79 Active campaigns, new malware with indicators, critical vulnerabilities, significant breaches 20–49 Breach and malware news without technical detail, structured intel without strong text signals, patched critical bugs 0–19 Round-ups, guides, product news, scam warnings (check their fraud score), routine leak-site postings

Webhooks use 70 as the default threshold for a "high severity" item, and AI auto-summaries only run from 40 upwards.

docs.title: Sharing and delivery
docs.text: This page explains the rules that decide what may leave JATMP, and how webhooks and MISP pushes are produced and delivered. The interfaces themselves (REST API, IOC feeds, STIX / TAXII, MISP) are described in Sharing and integrations. The code is in app/sharing.py, app/webhooks.py and app/intel/misp.py.

docs.title: One gate for everything that leaves
docs.text: The REST API, the IOC feeds, STIX bundles and TAXII collections, webhooks and MISP pushes all ask the same module, app/sharing.py, whether an item or indicator may leave. It applies three independent checks, and all three must pass.

docs.title: 1. TLP
docs.text:
Every item has an effective TLP, worked out in this order:

  1. the item's own TLP, if the feed provided one (OTX pulses, MISP events);
  2. otherwise, the TLP of its source (set under Settings → Sources);
  3. otherwise, CLEAR.

Values are normalised, so tlp:amber becomes AMBER, WHITE becomes CLEAR and AMBER+STRICT becomes AMBER. An item may be shared when its effective TLP is at or below the api_max_tlp setting (GREEN by default). With the default, AMBER and RED items never leave JATMP.

Because a source without a TLP counts as CLEAR, its items are shared. To make that a deliberate choice, the Add source form asks for a TLP and tells you whether the source's items will be shared, and Settings → Sharing & API shows how many sources have no TLP set.

docs.title: 2. Redistribution
docs.text:
Some providers' terms don't allow their data to be passed on, so each source has a "share outside JATMP" flag:

Flag Meaning Not set The default for the source type: everything is shared except ANY.RUN (provider terms) and ransomware.live (victim names stay in-house) On / off Set by an admin, overriding the default

Items from a source that may not be redistributed are never shared, whatever their TLP.

Provider details, meaning the answers from VirusTotal, ANY.RUN and the other enrichment providers (summaries, scores, raw data), only leave when an admin switches on api_share_provider_details. JATMP's own combined verdict can always be shared.

docs.title: 3. Personal data
docs.text: Scammer identifiers (phone numbers, bank accounts, e-wallets and crypto wallets) never leave JATMP. They are excluded from the API (asking for one by its id returns 404), the IOC feeds, STIX / TAXII, webhooks (even when someone watches one) and MISP pushes. See Scams and fraud.

docs.title: When can an indicator be shared?
docs.text:
An indicator can be shared when at least one shareable item mentions it, or when it was linked by a provider whose data may be passed on (OTX, ThreatFox, MalwareBazaar, URLhaus, MISP). For example, an IP that only ever appeared in an ANY.RUN task or an AMBER pulse is not exported, but the same IP mentioned in a public news article is.

Analysts' corrections carry through to what is shared. An indicator marked not a threat becomes clean, so it drops out of the feeds (which list malicious indicators by default), and an analyst's verdict is the one that is exported. A link an analyst removed no longer counts as a mention.

On top of that, the IOC export feeds and TAXII leave out IPs, domains and URLs whose malicious or suspicious verdict is older than verdict_feed_days (60 by default) and hasn't been confirmed since. That way a blocklist built from JATMP doesn't keep blocking addresses that have changed hands. See Verdicts that age.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Event Sent when What it contains item.high_severity A collection run stores an item with a severity of at least webhook_min_severity (default 70) The item: id, title, URL, severity, source and source type, TLP, publication time, up to 10 families / actors / CVEs, and a link into JATMP when public_base_url is set entity.watched A new item mentions an entity that any user is watching (scammer identifiers excepted) The item, plus the watched entity ioc.malicious An indicator's verdict turns malicious, through enrichment or because an analyst set it The indicator, with a link to it job.failed Any error notification is created: a source starts failing or has been failing for a day, an enrichment run fails, or the AI summary or a MISP push fails The notification's title and text

Item events are only sent for shareable items, and only during live collection: backfills send none. When ThreatFox adds new IOCs to an item it already stored, no new event is sent. A manual collection batch with failures produces a warning notification rather than an error, so it doesn't trigger job.failed. The failure notifications of scheduled runs do.

docs.title: From event to delivery
docs.text:
1. Queue. For every enabled webhook subscribed to the event, a delivery is saved as pending, with the payload {"event", "created_at", "data"}. Item events are queued right after the collection run has stored its items; the indicator event is queued in the same transaction as the new verdict.
  2. Deliver. run_webhooks runs every 30 seconds and sends up to 50 due deliveries, oldest first, saving the result after each one.
  3. Format. Generic webhooks receive the payload as JSON. Slack, Discord and Teams webhooks receive a ready-made message: a title, a line with source, severity and entities, and an Open link.
  4. Sign. Every request carries X-JATMP-Event, X-JATMP-Delivery (the delivery id), X-JATMP-Timestamp and X-JATMP-Signature: sha256=<HMAC-SHA256(secret, "<timestamp>.<body>")>. The secret is derived from the installation's secret key and the webhook's salt, so it is never stored in the database.
  5. Send. The request has a 10-second timeout, doesn't follow redirects, and goes through the outbound guard: private and loopback addresses are refused unless allow private webhook targets is on, and the connection is made to the address that was checked (so the name can't be switched to a different address in between).
  6. Retry. A 2xx response marks the delivery ok. Anything else is retried after 1 minute, 5 minutes, 30 minutes and 2 hours. If the fifth attempt also fails, the delivery is marked failed. Each webhook shows its last status.

Deliveries older than 30 days are deleted by the nightly housekeeping.

docs.title: Checking a webhook on the receiving side
docs.text: Recalculate HMAC-SHA256(secret, timestamp + "." + raw_body) and compare it with the signature, using a constant-time comparison. Reject requests whose timestamp is more than a few minutes old, to prevent replays, and use X-JATMP-Delivery to ignore a delivery you have already processed: a retry after a timeout can arrive twice.

docs.title: MISP push
docs.text:
How What is pushed Send to MISP on an item One event for the item: its title, TLP and family tags, with its indicators as attributes Send to MISP on a family or actor page One event for the entity, with its indicators Auto-push After each live collection run, every new item with a severity of at least misp_autopush_min_severity (0 = off)

An item is refused if it came from MISP (it is never pushed back), or if the sharing rules don't allow it. An item that has already been pushed isn't pushed again (the event is recorded on the item). Auto-push runs as its own job after the collection run, and a failure creates an error notification (at most one a day).

docs.title: Requests JATMP makes on its own
docs.text: Everything above is data JATMP publishes. JATMP also requests data: feeds, intel providers, CVE intel, the AI and GeoIP updates. All of those requests go through the outbound guard (netguard): only public addresses (unless a host is on the private allow-list), every redirect checked, the connection made to the address that was checked, and responses capped at 20 MB after decompression. Each request only sends what the lookup needs: an indicator to an intel provider, a CVE id to EPSS and the NVD, and, only when a cloud AI is configured, the prompts described in AI processing, with personal data replaced.

docs.title: Trends and correlation
docs.text: This page explains how the dashboards turn stored items into trend scores, CVE priorities, breakdowns and lists of related items. None of these figures are stored: they are calculated from the items whenever a page is opened (trend lists are cached for 45 seconds). The code is in app/processing/trends.py, app/processing/graph.py and app/intel/cve.py.

docs.title: Counting rules
docs.text:
Three rules decide what a number on the dashboards actually counts.

Stories, not copies. When several outlets publish the same article, the original and its copies count as one story (see Cross-source duplicates). This rule applies everywhere JATMP counts how much was reported:

  • the KPI tiles and their sparklines, and the timelines;
  • the breakdown charts (malware and actor types, sectors, scam types, brands);
  • target countries and provinces;
  • mention counts in the entity lists;
  • trend scores and the scam spreading check;
  • the AI executive summary and the PDF / Word reports.

The Stories collected tile also shows the number of items, copies included, when the two differ.

Per-outlet figures count items. Items per source, source countries and languages describe what each outlet published, so there a copy counts for the outlet that carried it.

Dates and regions. Periods are measured by publication date, so backfilled history lands in the period it was published in, not the day it was collected. In the National (ID) view, every figure only includes items that target Indonesia, or that come from an Indonesian outlet without naming another target (see The National view).

docs.title: Periods and baselines
docs.text:
Period Chart bars Trend baseline 7, 15 or 30 days One per day The 30 days before the period 3 months (90 days) One per day The 90 days before the period 6 months, 1 year One per week (the first day of each 7-day block) As long as the period itself

In other words, the baseline is always the max(30, period) days immediately before the period. The live collectors only cover the recent past, so the longer periods (and their baselines) only become meaningful after a backfill. The dashboards tell you when some sources have gaps.

docs.title: Trend score
docs.text:
Malware families, threat actors and CVEs on the threat radar, in the Trending tables and in the AI summary are ranked by a trend score. For one entity, with a period of W days and a baseline of B days, JATMP uses:

Input Meaning r Stories that mention it in the period b Stories that mention it in the baseline s How many different sources reported it in the period (originals only; at least 1) c How many different source types (news, social, intel) reported it in the period (at least 1) 
growth = (r / W + 0.1) / (b / B + 0.1)
score  = r × √min(growth, 10) × (1 + 0.25 × (s − 1)) × (1 + 0.2 × (c − 1))

Each part has a job:

  • Volume (r) is the starting point. Something mentioned only once doesn't trend, however new it is.
  • Growth compares the daily rate now with the daily rate before. The + 0.1 stops a first mention from producing infinite growth, and the square root and the cap at 10 stop a sudden spike from drowning out threats that are steady but widely covered.
  • Spread rewards independent confirmation: each extra source adds 25%, and each extra source type adds 20%. Syndicated copies don't count as extra sources.
Example (7-day period, 30-day baseline) r b s c growth score A family that suddenly shows up in the news and on Bluesky 6 3 4 2 4.79 27.56 A family that is always in the news at this rate 6 26 4 2 0.99 12.54 A single blog that mentions a new name twice 2 0 1 1 3.86 3.93 An outbreak that everyone covers 20 0 8 3 29.57 (capped at 10) 243.5

A few more rules:

  • An entity with no story in the period isn't listed at all.
  • A malware name that was only ever found by the "Name ransomware" pattern only appears once two sources name it in the period, so a single misread headline can't make something trend.
  • An entity first seen during the period gets the new badge. To list only such entities, use the ✦ New threats button on the Intelligence lists (Malware, Threat actors, CVEs, IOCs, Scam types, Impersonated brands), which keeps the entries whose first-seen date falls in the chosen period; see Using JATMP.
  • Actors are grouped by type (nation-state, ransomware, extortion, cybercrime or unclassified), using the knowledge base or a category you set in data/knowledge_extra.json.

Trend lists are cached in memory for 45 seconds for each combination of type, period, region and list length. The cache is cleared whenever a collection run stores new items.

docs.title: CVE priority
docs.text:
Lots of chatter about a vulnerability doesn't necessarily mean it should be patched first. So trending CVEs are re-ranked by how likely they are to be exploited:

priority = trend score × (2 if in CISA KEV) × (1 + EPSS) × (0.5 + CVSS / 10)

A CVE without a CVSS score is multiplied by 1 for that part. The dashboard takes the 60 CVEs with the highest trend scores, sorts them by priority, shows the top 8, and lists the families and actors mentioned alongside each one.

For example, take two CVEs that both have a trend score of 10. The first is in KEV, with an EPSS of 0.6 and a CVSS of 9.8: 10 × 2 × 1.6 × 1.48 = 47.4. The second isn't in KEV, with an EPSS of 0.01 and a CVSS of 5.3: 10 × 1 × 1.01 × 1.03 = 10.4.

docs.title: CVEs by exploitation risk
docs.text:
This chart puts each CVE mentioned in the period into the first bucket it qualifies for:

Bucket Condition In CISA KEV It is in the catalogue EPSS 10%+ Its EPSS score is 0.10 or more CVSS critical CVSS 9 or more CVSS high CVSS 7 to 8.9 CVSS medium / low Any other CVSS score Low EPSS, no CVSS Looked up, but none of the above (counted below the chart) Not looked up yet No CVE intel yet (counted below the chart)

The data comes from the CVE intel refresh.

docs.title: Correlation
docs.text:
The Correlated items card on an item's page (and in its preview) ranks other items by how strong the evidence they share is, not just by how many entities they have in common.

Each shared entity contributes:

weight(type) / log2(2 + mention_count)

so a rare entity counts for more than one that is mentioned everywhere.

Type Weight Type Weight sha256, sha1, md5 6.0 crypto wallet 6.0 url 5.0 bank account, e-wallet 5.0 domain 4.0 phone 4.0 ip 3.0 brand 1.0 malware, actor 2.5 scam type 0.5 cve 1.5 sector 0.2 technique 0.5

An item's score is the sum over all the entities it shares. It is then multiplied by 1.3 if the item comes from a different source type (a news article and a Bluesky post, say), or by 1.15 if it comes from a different source of the same type. Matches through an indicator are flagged as strong. The top 15 are shown.

Newsletters and round-ups. A digest (Cisco Talos' Threat Source, weekly round-ups, podcasts) covers several unrelated stories and repeats a "most prevalent files" list every issue, so what it shares with another item is weak evidence. JATMP treats an item as a digest when:

  • its source's config has "digest": true (false opts a source out, and then nothing else is checked). The source form in Settings has no field for it yet; it is kept in the source's stored config, and saving the form leaves it in place;
  • its title or tags use round-up wording (newsletter, threat source, week in review, roundup, bulletin, in other news, weekly threat report, daily briefing, mingguan, kilas siber…). Words that the scam and sector analysis treat as round-ups but that name a single story here (interview, as in the Contagious Interview campaign, lessons from, webinar) don't count;
  • or its body carries newsletter boilerplate (Welcome to this week's edition…, Upcoming events where you can find, most prevalent malware files). Talos issue titles such as "Never be afraid to ask questions" say nothing, so the title alone is not enough.

When one of the two items is a digest, the score is multiplied by 0.4, and by 0.1 when both are. Two issues of the same source are never linked (what they share is the recurring boilerplate), and a digest link whose discounted score falls below 1 is dropped before the source bonus above is applied. The links that remain carry a digest badge and are never flagged strong.

The flag is stored on the item (items.is_digest) when it is collected. After an upgrade that changes the detection rules, run_digesttag sets it again on every stored item, and manage.py digesttag does the same by hand (for example after changing a source's "digest" setting). An item whose text retention has already trimmed keeps a digest flag it had, since the body phrases that proved it are gone.

Co-mentions. Mentioned together with on an entity's page and in its preview, the indicators listed on a family's page, the related chips on the lists and the related list of GET /api/v1/entities/{id} count the entities that appear in the same items, and they leave out digests entirely: a hash from a newsletter's weekly most prevalent files list sits next to the family of another story, and that is no evidence the two belong together. Even outside digests, being in the same article is not attribution (on this deployment's data, an indicator and a family from the same article agreed with the provider's family only about a third of the time). So on an indicator's page the card is called Seen in the same items as and says so, and Linked by enrichment (what a provider attributes) is shown above it.

To keep this fast, entities mentioned in more than 400 items aren't used to find candidates (although they still add weight to candidates found through rarer entities), and at most the 4,000 most recent links are read.

docs.title: Relationship graph
docs.text:
The graph on an item's page is built from:

  1. the item itself, in the centre;
  2. its entities (indicators with a bad verdict first), taking up at most 45% of the nodes;
  3. whatever enrichment linked them to (a hash's family, a domain's IPs, a family's OTX indicators), at most 25% of the nodes;
  4. the top related items from the correlation above, with lines to the entities they share.

On an entity's page, the graph shows the entity, its enrichment links, the families, actors and CVEs most often mentioned with it, and the 10 highest-severity items that mention it. The graph starts with up to 60 nodes; Show more raises the limit to 150. When something had to be left out, the graph says so.

Reading the lines. Under the graph, a second legend row shows each kind of line that appears in it, what it means and whose claim it is. Hover an entry for the explanation; hovering a line in the graph shows its label and the same claim.

Line Means Claim Solid, grey (Mentions) The item names the entity: extracted from its text by the platform's rules, or listed by the source's own indicator feed automatic Dashed, green (Provider link) A threat-intel provider (OTX, urlscan, MalwareBazaar…) states the relation, such as an indicator attributed to a family provider's claim Solid, blue (Also mentions) Another item names the same entity: not proof that the two items describe the same activity needs validation Dotted (Mentioned together) Two entities named in the same items: not attribution needs validation

Needs validation marks relations that come from co-occurrence only. An analyst can remove a wrong link with Correct (Analyst corrections). Newsletters and round-ups are left out of Mentioned together; an Also mentions line can still lead to one, because those lines come from the correlation above, where a digest counts for less.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to JATMP. Upgrade steps per version are in docs/upgrading.md.

docs.title: Unreleased
docs.text:
Changes

  • Scam reports are now the second feed, next to cyber threats, like the two dashboards: Feed → Scams & fraud (/feed/scams), with tabs on the Feed page to switch. They left the Intelligence dropdown; /fraud/items forwards to the new address with its filters.

Security

  • The REST endpoint for a single entity (/api/v1/entities/{id}) returned scammer phone numbers and bank accounts; identifiers now give 404 there too, like everywhere else they are never shared.
  • The stylesheet cleaner (0.10) could backtrack exponentially on crafted text and hang a collector thread for hours. It now parses selectors without nested quantifiers and looks for rules from their declaration block, in linear time.
  • Outbound guard for every request JATMP makes on its own (feeds, WordPress and Wayback backfill, RSS-Bridge, providers, CVE intel, the AI, MISP, GeoIP, webhooks): only public addresses unless a host is allow-listed, checked on every redirect hop, connecting to the checked address (no DNS rebinding), and bodies capped after decompression (no memory exhaustion by a huge feed or a gzip bomb; the GeoIP unpacking is capped too).
  • CSV reports and the CSV IOC feed neutralise cells that a spreadsheet would run as a formula.
  • AI output is bounded: at most +20 severity, shown as AI assessment; new families from a single news item are ignored until another source reports them; AI-proposed entities and tags carry an AI badge; tags are cleaned.
  • Manual enrichment, context lookups, deep dives and AI summaries are limited per user and minute and run once per entity at a time; Run now on a source is ignored while that source runs.
  • First-run setup from another machine requires a one-time token from the log or data/setup-token.
  • API keys, the AI key and the Telegram session are stored encrypted (Fernet, key from data/config.json).
  • Changing a password, an admin resetting it, or the new Sign out other sessions button ends the user's other sessions.
  • requirements.lock pins every dependency (Docker and CI install with it), CI runs pip-audit, Dependabot is on.
  • /healthz no longer reveals the version.

Data processing

  • Scammer identifiers need a cue that names the scammer; a generic "hubungi nomor" next to a police station, branch office or complaint line is not one. Crypto wallets must pass their checksum, and "alamat"/"address" no longer count as a crypto cue.
  • Weak scam phrases need a scam word nearby, and a malware article with one passing scam sentence is no longer a scam report. A brand that issues the warning is not counted as impersonated.
  • "Rp 2,5 T" and "Rp 5 M" are read as trillions and billions of rupiah.
  • Families and actors that are everyday words (Bitter, Patchwork, Pegasus, Oyster, Interlock…) need a qualifier; actors now follow the same rule. Demonyms and platform names ("the Indonesian ransomware gang", "Facebook malware") are no new family, a guessed family scores less than a known one, and it only trends once two sources name it. Intel-feed tags name families only on intel sources and never as everyday words.
  • Family names from providers and the AI pass the extractor's filters; Indonesian patterns also run on mixed- language items.
  • A sector needs more than one word in the title (unless the headline is about an attack on that one sector), and "bank", "rekening", "nasabah" in a scam report are the victim's bank, not an attacked finance sector.
  • Syndicated copies of a story from other outlets are marked as such: trending, spread velocity and the executive summary count the story once.
  • "critical" only scores next to a vulnerability ("critical flaw"), not in "critical infrastructure".
  • Long entry ids (URLs with tracking parameters) are hashed instead of cut at 500 characters, so they no longer collide. Re-scoring passes each link's origin, so a heuristic family scores the same as at ingest.
